# Chapter 1  INTRODUCTION

## Background of the Study

Lipa City is one of the fastest-growing urban centers in Calabarzon, serving as a major hub for commerce, industry, and tertiary education in the province of Batangas. Its rapid economic expansion has attracted a substantial residential and transient population, placing increasing strain on road networks that were not originally designed to handle high-density commuter flows. A study by Caraos, Montalbo, and Fillone (2023), published in the Proceedings of the Eastern Asia Society for Transportation Studies, confirms that Lipa City already generates approximately 147,132 daily one-way person-trips, with total registered vehicles reaching 138,087 as of 2020 and growing at an annual rate of 8.31 percent between 2015 and 2020 (Philippine Statistics Authority, as cited in Caraos et al., 2023). The same study notes that intracity jeepneys in Lipa operate at a mean speed of only 20 km/h, underscoring the capacity pressures already placed on the city's primary arterial roads.

For students and daily commuters in Lipa, travel time has become increasingly difficult to predict. Heavy tropical rainfall, a recurring seasonal condition across Batangas, consistently degrades road conditions, reduces vehicular speeds, and amplifies congestion beyond what standard navigation tools are capable of reflecting. While no published study has yet quantified rainfall-induced travel delays specifically within Lipa City, existing Philippine transport research documents analogous patterns in other urban contexts. Sunga, Diaz, and Napalang (2017) found that heavy rainfall caused 39.33 percent of commuters in Metro Manila to shift transport modes entirely, rising to 44.67 percent during intense rain events. Ibasco and Fillone (2016) further documented that 70 percent of university students in Manila departed immediately upon class suspension announcements, generating sudden surges in commuter demand that severely disrupted travel time predictability. These behavioral patterns are consistent with conditions observed in Lipa City, where comparable disruptions such as class cancellations at major institutions including Batangas State University Pablo Borbon and De La Salle Lipa, road closures caused by accidents, and logistical disruptions associated with local public events compound the unpredictability of daily commutes. The resulting delays carry concrete consequences: missed academic schedules, lateness to professional appointments, reduced productivity, and a generalized erosion of commuter well-being.

Existing navigation platforms such as Google Maps and Waze provide real-time traffic estimates and route optimization; however, their utility within Lipa City is limited by two structural gaps. First, their routing algorithms apply generalized speed parameters that do not account for the distinct operational characteristics of motorcycles, which are able to filter through congested traffic in ways enclosed private vehicles cannot, a behavioral pattern that deviates significantly from the performance profiles used by global mapping services and is consistent with the corridor-level congestion documented by Caraos et al. (2023) for Lipa City's primary arterial roads. As a result, estimated times of arrival computed using car-based routing assumptions alone are systematically inaccurate for motorcycle trips. Second, global navigation platforms are not configured to incorporate hyper-local disruption signals specific to Lipa City, including class cancellations at major academic institutions, localized accident reports at key intersections, or schedule-altering events tied to the city's commercial or cultural calendar.

To address these structural gaps, this study proposes the development of Transync, an intelligent predictive travel advisory system designed specifically for the road network and commuter profile of Lipa City. Transync moves beyond conventional GPS functionality by combining deterministic routing data from the Google Maps Platform with a real-time weather analysis pipeline using the Open-Meteo API, and an artificial intelligence advisory layer powered by Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6 language model. This architecture enables the system to compute vehicle-specific estimated times of arrival, apply learned corrections derived from live environmental and situational variables , and deliver contextualized departure-time recommendations to users. The entire pipeline is deployed within a cloud-based infrastructure to ensure real-time responsiveness, scalability, and reliability under varying load conditions.

Following the Capstone 1 defense panel evaluation conducted in April 2026, the system has been substantially enhanced for Capstone 2\. The deterministic weighted delay algorithm originally proposed in Chapter 3 of the Capstone 1 paper has been replaced by a supervised machine learning model specifically, an XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model trained on a proprietary corpus of logged trip records, weather snapshots, and curated Lipa-specific contextual events. This learned model predicts the P10, P50, and P90 corrections to the Google Maps Platform's baseline estimated time of arrival, enabling calibrated probabilistic departure-time recommendations rather than point estimates with imprecise confidence claims. The system has further been extended with a departure-time-given-arrival recommendation function, multi-stop trip composition that supports user-specified dwell times, a five-tier API failure fallback strategy, a retrieval-augmented advisory layer that surfaces curated Lipa-specific context to the Claude Sonnet 4.6 module, and a native Android client built on Flutter that coexists alongside the original mobile-first web application. Each of these enhancements directly addresses one or more items from the Capstone 1 panel evaluation, and each is documented in detail in subsequent chapters of this revised paper. 

## Statement of the Problem

### General Problem

Commuters in Lipa City currently lack a localized, intelligent tool capable of accurately predicting optimal departure times by synthesizing real-time traffic conditions, meteorological data, and sudden urban disruptions into personalized travel advisories.

### Specific Problems

1. Existing navigation platforms apply generalized speed parameters that fail to reflect the distinct operational realities of public utility vehicles in Lipa City, and no local data infrastructure exists to systematically collect the trip records, weather snapshots, and contextual events necessary to train a locally calibrated predictive correction model.  
> 2. No localized machine learning model exists for Lipa City that learns vehicle-type-aware delay patterns from historical trip data and produces calibrated probabilistic arrival estimates across varying operational conditions, leaving commuters with point-estimate travel times that misrepresent the true uncertainty of travel in a rainfall-prone, event-disrupted urban environment.  
> 3. Commuters currently have no tool capable of computing a reliable departure time given a target arrival, especially for multi-stop trips with intermediate dwell times, forcing them to rely on manual estimation that systematically underestimates compounding delays across trip legs.  
> 4. Existing travel advisory systems in the Philippine secondary-city context lack a rigorous, scientifically grounded evaluation framework that quantifies prediction reliability through quantile coverage, classification accuracy, and statistically validated performance comparisons against established baselines.  
> 5. No existing platform integrates hyper-local Lipa-specific disruption signals such as LGU traffic advisories, school dismissal schedules, fiesta calendars, and market day patterns into a live advisory layer, nor provides graceful degradation behavior that maintains system utility when one or more external data sources fail.  
> 6. Current navigation tools offer no native Android application tailored to the Lipa City commuter context, limiting accessibility for users whose primary device usage favors native mobile applications over browser-based interfaces.

   

## Statement of the Objectives

General Objective

This study aims to design, develop, and empirically validate an intelligent predictive travel advisory system for Lipa City, Batangas, that delivers calibrated probabilistic departure-time recommendations through a residual-correction supervised machine learning model trained on locally collected trip data, integrated with a retrieval-augmented contextual advisory layer, and deployed across both a mobile-first web application and a native Android client. y.

Specific Objectives

1. Data Infrastructure. To construct a structured data collection pipeline that persists every Google Maps Directions API response, every Open-Meteo weather snapshot, and every completed user trip's actual duration into a relational SQLite training corpus, and to produce a derived training data table suitable as input for supervised machine learning.  
> 2. Predictive Model. To develop an XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model that predicts the P10, P50, and P90 deviations of actual trip duration from the Google Maps Platform's baseline estimated time of arrival, conditioned on temporal, meteorological, geometric, vehicle-type, and Lipa-specific contextual features, and to demonstrate statistically significant improvement in mean absolute error over the Google Maps baseline on a temporally held-out test set.  
> 3. Departure-Time Recommendation Algorithm. To implement a departure-time recommendation algorithm that, given a user-specified target arrival time and route, returns the latest viable departure time at a user-selected confidence level, with explicit support for multi-stop trips composed of user-specified intermediate dwell times at each stop.  
> 4. Quantitative Evaluation Methodology. To establish a quantitative evaluation methodology that validates the predictive model using mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and mean absolute percentage error per quantile, quantile coverage proximity to target percentile, and a confusion matrix derived from an early/on-time/late classification framing on test predictions, with all reported metrics accompanied by ninety-five percent confidence intervals computed via paired bootstrap resampling.  
> 5. Local Context and Fallback Integration. To integrate Lipa-specific local data sources including Local Government Unit traffic advisories, school dismissal schedules, fiesta and payday calendars, and market day patterns into a retrieval-augmented advisory layer powered by the Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 language model, and to implement a five-tier graceful degradation strategy that ensures the system continues to deliver useful output during partial or complete external API failure.  
> 6. Cross-Platform Deployment. To deploy the complete Transync system across both the existing mobile-first web application built on Next.js and a new native Android client built on Flutter, with both clients calling a shared Node.js and Express backend integrated with the Python FastAPI machine learning microservice.

   

## Significance of the Study

The development of Transync addresses a concrete and underserved gap in urban mobility infrastructure within Lipa City. Its contributions extend across multiple stakeholder groups.

For Commuters and the Student Population. The primary beneficiaries of this research are daily travelers and students within Lipa's academic hub. By providing departure-time recommendations that account for vehicle-specific behavior, learned local context corrections, and calibrated probabilistic arrival estimates rather than vague point estimates, the system enables users to make proactive scheduling decisions rather than reactive adjustments. This is particularly significant during periods of heavy tropical rainfall or sudden class suspensions, which currently generate considerable unpredictability in commute planning. The addition of a native Android client further broadens accessibility to commuters whose primary device usage favors native mobile applications, while the multi-modal estimated time of arrival capability ensures relevance across different economic strata, whether users rely on private cars or motorcycles. 

For Local Transportation Authorities and Urban Planners. This study provides a functional blueprint for evidence-based traffic management within the context of a rapidly urbanizing secondary city. Caraos et al. (2023) have identified Lipa City as a critical case requiring immediate transport intervention before its congestion patterns become as intractable as those of Metro Manila. By demonstrating how heterogeneous data streams including Google Maps traffic density, Open-Meteo meteorological data, and curated Lipa-specific contextual events can be synthesized into calibrated, actionable commuter guidance through supervised machine learning and constrained generative artificial intelligence, the research offers a replicable framework applicable to smart city initiatives within the province of Batangas and beyond. 

For the Field of Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence Research. This research contributes to the applied body of knowledge on hybrid deterministic and supervised machine learning architectures within domain-specific advisory systems. By layering an XGBoost quantile residual correction model on top of an established commercial routing engine, and by employing a constrained large language model exclusively as an interpretive advisory layer over structured analytical outputs rather than as a replacement for deterministic routing logic, the study demonstrates a defensible hybrid architecture that extends utility beyond either pure deterministic computation or unconstrained generative reasoning. It establishes an empirical precedent for how calibrated probabilistic machine learning models and constrained artificial intelligence modules can together bridge global mapping services and the operational realities of Philippine secondary-city road environments. 

For Future Researchers. This study documents a complete technical methodology, evaluation framework, and revision tracking discipline suitable for application in other rapidly developing Philippine cities facing analogous infrastructure and weather-related travel challenges. The data infrastructure schema, feature engineering specification, quantile regression methodology, and graceful fallback strategy collectively serve as a scalable template for related research at the intersection of urban mobility, applied machine learning, and constrained artificial intelligence integration, providing future researchers with a reproducible foundation that is honest about its limitations and rigorous in its validation standards. 

## Scope and Delimitations

This study encompasses the design, development, and functional validation of Transync as a cloud-native predictive travel advisory system optimized for the urban road network of Lipa City, Batangas. The system is built on a data pipeline that ingests real-time traffic density from the Google Maps Platform, meteorological data from the Open-Meteo API, and curated Lipa-specific contextual events maintained in a local SQLite knowledge base. Predictive correction is handled by an XGBoost quantile regression residual model trained on a locally collected trip corpus and deployed as a Python FastAPI microservice. Advisory generation is handled by Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6 language model, which interprets structured computational outputs from the deterministic routing layer, the quantile regression correction model, and the retrieval-augmented Lipa context layer into human-readable departure recommendations and risk notifications. 

The system generates estimated times of arrival that differentiate between private cars and motorcycles through vehicle-type-aware features within a single shared predictive model. It supports multi-stop itinerary planning with user-specified dwell times at each intermediate stop, alternate route generation, calibrated probabilistic departure-time recommendations at user-selected confidence levels, and real-time advisory updates. The system is delivered through two parallel client platforms: a mobile-first web application built on Next.js and a native Android application built on Flutter. Validation is conducted with thirty confirmed User Acceptance Testing participants within the 2025 to 2026 academic year, with primary focus on high-traffic corridors and critical intersections within Lipa City's urban center. 

The delimitations of the study restrict the scope to vehicular traffic flows and exclude pedestrian mobility, cycling, and fixed public transportation scheduling data such as formal jeepney or bus timetables. Geographically, predictive modeling is confined to internal arterial roads within Lipa City; the system does not extend to intercity transportation dynamics or to major expressways including the STAR Tollway. The system relies exclusively on third-party application programming interface integrations without incorporating physical Internet of Things devices or locally deployed traffic sensors. The native client is delimited to the Android platform; cross-platform deployment is not part of delimitation. The research also does not encompass large-scale public deployment or integration with government infrastructure beyond conceptual applicability, as the deliverable is a functional prototype validated under controlled conditions with thirty confirmed User Acceptance Testing participants. 

## Definition of Terms

The following terms are defined as they are used within the context of this study.

Application Programming Interface \- A structured set of protocols and communication rules that enables distinct software systems to exchange data and functionality. In this study, application programming interfaces serve as the primary channels through which Transync retrieves real-time traffic data from the Google Maps Platform, meteorological conditions from the Open-Meteo API, and artificial intelligence advisory outputs from Anthropic. The reliability and latency of these integrations are critical determinants of overall system performance.

Claude Sonnet 4.6. \- A large language model developed by Anthropic, released in February 2026, and accessible via the Anthropic application programming interface using the model identifier claude-sonnet-4-6. In this system, Claude Sonnet 4.6 functions as a constrained interpretive advisory module: it receives structured numerical outputs from the deterministic routing layer, the quantile regression correction model, and the retrieval-augmented Lipa context layer, and generates human-readable departure recommendations and risk-level notifications. It does not perform routing calculations and is not configured to produce outputs beyond the defined advisory scope. 

Departure Time Prediction \- A computational output that calculates the recommended time for a commuter to begin travel in order to arrive at a destination by a specified time, accounting for the Google Maps Platform baseline estimated time of arrival, the XGBoost quantile residual correction predicted at a user-selected confidence level, and any user-specified dwell times at intermediate stops. This differs from a simple estimated time of arrival in that it is an action-oriented recommendation generated in advance of departure rather than a passive estimate during travel. 

Deterministic Routing \- A navigation computation approach in which route selection and estimated time of arrival calculation are based on fixed mathematical algorithms applied to structured inputs such as distance, average speed, and traffic density. In this system, deterministic routing is provided by the Google Maps Platform and serves as the factual foundation over which artificial intelligence interpretation is layered.

Estimated Time of Arrival \- The projected time at which a commuter is expected to reach a specified destination given a defined origin, route, and set of traffic and environmental conditions. In Transync, estimated times of arrival are computed via the Google Maps Platform as a baseline value, then corrected by the XGBoost quantile residual model to produce calibrated P10, P50, and P90 estimates reflecting optimistic, typical, and conservative arrival scenarios respectively. 

Large Language Model \- A class of artificial intelligence model trained on large-scale text corpora to perform natural language understanding and generation tasks. Large language models such as Claude Sonnet 4.6 are capable of contextual reasoning over structured inputs when properly constrained through system-level prompting. In transportation advisory applications, large language models function most reliably as interpretive layers rather than as replacement components for deterministic computations.

Live Advisory \- A real-time, system-generated notification delivered to the user in response to a sudden change in travel conditions. Live advisories in Transync are triggered by events such as road closures, class suspension announcements, or significant deterioration in weather or traffic conditions, and are expressed in natural language generated by the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory layer informed by the retrieval-augmented Lipa context. 

Multi-Modal Estimated Time of Arrival \- A set of differentiated estimated times of arrival computed for multiple transportation modes simultaneously. In this study, multi-modal estimated times of arrival are generated for two vehicle categories: private cars and motorcycles, differentiated through a vehicle-type feature and its interaction terms within the XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model, informed by the corridor-level congestion patterns documented by Caraos et al. (2023) for Lipa City roads.

Open-Meteo API \- A free, keyless weather data platform that provides real-time and forecasted meteorological data including precipitation intensity, visibility, temperature, wind speed, and weather condition classifications. The free tier offers 10,000 calls per day for non-commercial use, with data available on demand, making it suitable for prototype-scale applications. In this system, the Open-Meteo API supplies the environmental variables used as features within the XGBoost quantile residual model. 

System Usability Scale \- A standardized ten-item Likert-scale questionnaire developed by Brooke (1986) used to measure the perceived usability of a system. System Usability Scale scores range from 0 to 100, with scores of 70 and above considered acceptable usability. This instrument is used in this study as the primary quantitative measure for User Acceptance Testing outcomes.

Weighted Delay \- A quantified time penalty added to the baseline estimated time of arrival in the Capstone 1 prototype to reflect adverse conditions such as heavy rainfall or road closures. The weighted delay algorithm has been superseded in Capstone 2 by the XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model, which learns delay patterns from historical trip data rather than applying manually assigned penalty weights. 

Confusion Matrix. A tabular evaluation tool used in classification analysis that displays the counts of predicted versus actual class assignments. In this study, the confusion matrix is computed on a three-class framing  early, on-time, and late  derived from the quantile regression model's P10 and P90 boundaries, providing a direct diagnostic of quantile calibration accuracy.

Quantile Coverage. An evaluation metric for quantile regression models that measures the fraction of test observations whose actual outcome falls at or below the model's predicted quantile. For a well-calibrated model, the empirical coverage approximates the nominal quantile. This metric replaces the imprecise plus or minus five minute accuracy claim from the Capstone 1 paper.

Quantile Regression. A statistical method introduced by Koenker and Bassett (1978) that predicts a specified percentile of the conditional distribution of an outcome variable rather than its conditional mean. In this study, quantile regression is performed using the XGBoost library configured with the reg:quantileerror objective and three quantile targets: P10, P50, and P90.

Residual Correction Model. A supervised machine learning model whose prediction target is the residual  the error  of a baseline reference system rather than the absolute outcome itself. In this study, the residual correction model is trained to predict the difference between actual trip duration and the Google Maps Platform's baseline estimated time of arrival.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation. A pattern for augmenting large language model outputs by retrieving relevant external knowledge at inference time and injecting that knowledge into the model's prompt. In this study, retrieval-augmented generation is implemented through structured SQL queries against the lipa\_context\_events table, supplying the Claude Sonnet 4.6 module with curated Lipa-specific disruption context on every advisory request.

SHAP. SHapley Additive exPlanations, a model interpretability framework introduced by Lundberg and Lee (2017) that assigns each input feature an importance value for each individual prediction. In this study, SHAP analysis is applied to the XGBoost quantile residual model to produce ranked feature importance and partial dependence diagnostics, providing a scientifically grounded basis for understanding which variables most influence departure-time predictions.

XGBoost. Extreme Gradient Boosting, a supervised machine learning library released by Chen and Guestrin (2016) that implements gradient-boosted decision tree ensembles. XGBoost is the algorithmic framework underlying the residual correction model in this study, selected for its competitive predictive performance on tabular data, computational efficiency, and compatibility with quantile regression objectives.

# Chapter 2 REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES

## Introduction

In rapidly urbanizing cities such as Lipa City, increasing congestion and weather-related variability significantly affect travel time reliability, particularly for students and daily commuters. Rainfall and environmental disruptions are shown to reduce vehicular speed and increase delay unpredictability, highlighting the limitations of purely deterministic routing systems. While platforms like Google Maps provide optimized routes and real-time traffic data, they operate primarily on structured algorithmic outputs without fully synthesizing contextual, behavioral, and environmental variables into predictive commuter guidance.

To address this gap, this project proposes a hybrid navigation architecture that integrates deterministic geospatial application programming interfaces with a supervised machine learning correction layer and an artificial intelligence interpretive layer. Consistent with findings by Zhou et al. (2023), the large language model functions not as a replacement for routing algorithms but as a contextual reasoning layer that translates structured traffic data into actionable, personalized recommendations. By incorporating temporal patterns, historical trip data, environmental conditions, and real-time disruptions, the system transitions from reactive navigation to proactive mobility forecasting. This approach is further supported by Huang et al. (2022), who show that context-aware road travel time estimation improves prediction by integrating spatial, temporal, and congestion-related context, reinforcing the value of localized and data-integrated commuter advisory systems. 

Weather-Integrated Spatiotemporal Traffic Forecasting

Zhang et al. (2023) developed a spatiotemporal graph convolutional network incorporating precipitation intensity and temperature variance into traffic speed forecasting using the PEMS-BAY dataset. Their model achieved a measurable reduction in mean absolute error compared to traffic-only baselines, demonstrating that exogenous weather variables significantly enhance predictive stability under fluctuating road conditions. However, the framework remained predictive in nature and did not operationalize results into commuter-facing advisory outputs. This gap highlights the need for systems that transform weather-sensitive forecasts into actionable departure-time guidance.

Extreme Weather Impact Modeling in Urban Corridors

Tang et al. (2024) proposed a hazard-aware traffic prediction framework combining environmental severity indices with deep temporal learning models. Their findings show improved responsiveness during heavy rainfall and low-visibility conditions compared to traditional long short-term memory models. Despite improved detection of disruption patterns, the study did not address real-time advisory dissemination. This limitation underscores the importance of integrating predictive analytics with decision-support layers for commuter applications.

Attention-Based Traffic-Weather Data Fusion

Nasser et al. (2023) introduced a multi-head attention mechanism to fuse traffic flow data with meteorological signals. Evaluation on urban datasets demonstrated enhanced short-term prediction accuracy under adverse weather scenarios. While the architecture improved forecasting reliability, it did not explore interpretative reasoning layers for translating structured outputs into user-centered advisories. This gap supports the rationale for layering deterministic mapping data with an artificial intelligence interpretive module.

Dynamic Graph Neural Networks for Urban Traffic

Li et al. (2022) proposed a dynamic graph neural network modeling evolving road-network dependencies across time. Tested against METR-LA and PEMS datasets, the model outperformed static adjacency frameworks in capturing nonstationary congestion trends. Although effective for forecasting, the system focused exclusively on predictive accuracy rather than decision-support integration. This highlights the absence of commuter-oriented translation mechanisms in advanced forecasting literature.

Causal Graph Attention in Traffic Prediction

Zhao et al. (2022) presented a spatiotemporal causal graph attention model capable of capturing inter-node dependencies in complex urban systems. Experimental evaluation demonstrated improved robustness against abrupt traffic fluctuations. However, the study remained confined to modeling improvements and did not address interpretability for end users. The need for advisory-level explanation remains unaddressed in such high-performance models.

Travel Time Estimation Using Application Programming Interface Data Streams

Peer, Tomori, Wagner, and Winkler (2025) analyzed the relationship between Google Maps travel time estimates and actual travel times reported by commuters in a stated preference study conducted in Vienna. Their findings indicate that respondents consistently perceived real-life travel times as longer than the corresponding Google Maps estimates, with discrepancies ranging from two to eleven percent across transport modes. The study attributes these gaps primarily to time overhead factors not captured by the platform's routing algorithm, such as parking search time and mode-specific behavioral variation. These findings validate deterministic mapping services as a practical real-time routing foundation while establishing that their raw outputs require contextual interpretation to reflect the travel experience of commuters accurately, particularly under heterogeneous traffic conditions.

Reliability Assessment of Navigation Application Programming Interface Outputs

Bastarianto et al. (2025) assessed inconsistencies in travel time outputs derived from Google Maps in developing-city contexts, using travel diary survey data from Greater Jakarta. Their findings reveal that discrepancies between application programming interface-derived travel attributes and traveler-reported data can introduce systematic bias into transport behavior modeling. The study demonstrates that even minor adjustments to which observations are included during data pre-processing can substantially alter travel time savings estimates, emphasizing contextual sensitivity and potential variability in congestion reporting. This supports the architectural separation between deterministic routing provided by mapping services and higher-level reasoning layers capable of interpreting delay differentials for commuter advisories, particularly in developing-country urban environments analogous to Lipa City.

Departure Time Behavioral Modeling

Zannat et al. (2022) investigated commuter departure-time decisions under congestion uncertainty, demonstrating that travelers adjust schedules based on anticipated delay costs and reliability thresholds. Their findings suggest that predictive guidance can meaningfully influence commuter behavior when reliability information is transparent. This behavioral evidence directly supports the value of predictive departure recommendation systems.

Real-Time Intelligent Transportation System Frameworks in Smart Cities

Dmitrieva et al. (2024) explored cloud-based intelligent transportation system infrastructures emphasizing real-time data ingestion and low-latency processing. Their framework separates sensing, computation, and advisory layers, advocating modular architectures. This aligns with hybrid deterministic-artificial intelligence designs where routing remains computationally stable while interpretive layers enhance guidance.

Cloud-Native Traffic Advisory Architectures

Chen et al. (2024) proposed a microservice-based traffic management framework leveraging cloud-native scalability and application programming interface orchestration. Their study emphasizes modular separation between routing engines and decision-support modules. This architectural principle mirrors the deterministic backend combined with the Claude Sonnet 4.6 interpretive layer implemented in Transync.

Large Language Models in Transportation Decision Support

Wandelt et al. (2024) reviewed large language model applications in transportation systems, identifying roles in contextual explanation, policy interpretation, and advisory reasoning. The study cautions against replacing deterministic computation with generative models and instead recommends hybrid integration. This supports the structured use of Claude Sonnet 4.6 as an interpretive advisory layer within Transync, where the model is constrained to generating natural language advisories over pre-computed deterministic outputs rather than performing routing logic independently.

Evaluating Large Language Model Performance in Structured Transportation Planning Tasks

A study published in GIScience and Remote Sensing evaluated the performance of large language models on structured transportation planning tasks across three assessment levels: geospatial reasoning, transport domain knowledge, and real-world decision support. Results indicate that larger general-purpose models achieved strong performance on structured decision support tasks, with 91 percent accuracy in real-world transport planning contexts when inputs were well-defined and constrained. The study reinforces the finding that large language models function most reliably when applied as structured copilots rather than autonomous decision-makers, and recommends hybrid artificial intelligence architectures that integrate language model reasoning with domain-specific analytical pipelines. These findings directly support the design decision in Transync to restrict Claude Sonnet 4.6 to advisory generation over deterministic routing outputs, rather than assigning it routing responsibility (Beyond Words, 2025).

Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Urban Mobility Systems

Wang et al. (2024) investigated explainable artificial intelligence mechanisms in mobility analytics, emphasizing transparency in risk communication. Their findings suggest that users trust systems more when reasoning outputs are clearly contextualized. This directly supports integrating Claude Sonnet 4.6 to enhance interpretability of congestion and weather metrics for commuters in Lipa City.

Multi-Source Data Integration in Intelligent Transportation Systems

Nguyen et al. (2023) explored multi-source data fusion combining traffic density, weather feeds, and temporal indicators. Their experimental framework showed improved reliability over single-source systems. However, the study did not extend findings into commuter advisory delivery. This gap motivates the operationalization of predictive insights into real-time, user-facing advisory outputs as implemented in Transync.

Adaptive Traffic Flow Modeling

Ma et al. (2024) introduced an evolutionary graph learning approach capturing dynamic congestion propagation patterns. Their evaluation confirms adaptability under changing road-network conditions. Despite predictive sophistication, the framework lacks user-facing advisory integration, reinforcing the importance of the decision-support layer that Transync implements through its XGBoost quantile residual correction model and artificial intelligence advisory module. 

Urban Congestion Risk Scoring Models

Kumar et al. (2023) developed probabilistic risk scoring systems for urban congestion during peak events. Their models estimate disruption likelihood rather than deterministic delay alone. This supports incorporating structured risk metrics as inputs to artificial intelligence-based advisory reasoning, a design principle that underlies Transync's use of Lipa-specific contextual event features within the quantile regression model. 

Human-Centered Navigation System Adoption

Gumasing et al. (2023) examined determinants of navigation application adoption in Southeast Asia using a technology acceptance framework. Their findings emphasize perceived usefulness and clarity of advisories as key adoption drivers. This validates the importance of user-centered advisory presentation in Transync, particularly for the student and commuter population in Lipa City whose adoption behavior mirrors the Southeast Asian context studied.

Integrated Smart Mobility Platforms

The World Bank (2024) highlights digital integration and predictive analytics as central to urban congestion mitigation in emerging cities. The report emphasizes transitioning from reactive monitoring to proactive mobility management. This policy-level framing contextualizes predictive departure systems within broader smart mobility objectives and reinforces the relevance of Transync as a practical intervention within the developing-city context of Lipa City.

Hybrid Deterministic-Artificial Intelligence Systems in Infrastructure

Garcia et al. (2023) examined hybrid system architectures combining deterministic simulation models with artificial intelligence interpretive modules. Their findings show improved decision-making transparency compared to purely predictive systems. This validates the hybrid approach implemented in Transync, where Google Maps deterministic routing and Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory generation operate as complementary rather than competing components.

Context-Aware Advisory Systems

Morales and Rivera (2022) investigated adaptive commuter advisory systems in Southeast Asian cities, demonstrating improved punctuality when advisories integrate congestion and environmental context. Their study reinforces the practical impact of predictive, context-sensitive travel guidance, and provides direct regional evidence that the advisory approach underlying Transync is applicable and effective within the Southeast Asian urban context.

Quantile Regression for Travel Time Prediction

> Koenker and Bassett (1978) established the foundational statistical framework of quantile regression, defining the pinball loss function and demonstrating that minimizing this asymmetric loss produces estimates of conditional quantiles of the outcome distribution rather than its conditional mean. This framework enables predictive models to report not just a single point estimate but a range of calibrated probabilistic outcomes corresponding to user-specified confidence levels. In the context of travel time prediction, quantile regression is particularly valuable because trip duration distributions are inherently skewed by adverse conditions a minority of trips under heavy rainfall or near road closures take substantially longer than the median. The Transync predictive model adopts this framework to report P10, P50, and P90 corrected arrival estimates, directly replacing the imprecise plus or minus five minute accuracy claim of the Capstone 1 prototype with a statistically grounded uncertainty representation.

Gradient-Boosted Trees for Tabular Prediction

> Chen and Guestrin (2016) introduced XGBoost as a scalable, regularized implementation of gradient-boosted decision tree ensembles, demonstrating competitive predictive performance on tabular data while maintaining computational efficiency and interpretability. These properties justify its selection over deep neural network approaches for the Transync use case, where training data is tabular, data scale is small to medium, and inference latency must remain under 3,000 milliseconds per request. Shwartz-Ziv and Armon (2022) further empirically demonstrate that gradient-boosted trees consistently outperform deep learning methods on tabular regression tasks at small-to-medium data scales, validating the architectural choice of XGBoost over deep sequence models for the residual correction task. Together these findings establish that the Transync predictive model is methodologically well-positioned within the current machine learning literature for its specific data characteristics and operational constraints.

SHAP for Model Interpretability

> Lundberg and Lee (2017) introduced SHapley Additive exPlanations as a unified framework for interpreting machine learning model predictions, assigning each input feature an importance value for each individual prediction derived from cooperative game theory. Unlike global feature importance measures, SHAP values provide local explanations that reveal why a specific prediction was made, enabling both model debugging and end-user transparency. In the context of Transync, SHAP analysis is applied to the trained XGBoost quantile residual model to produce ranked feature importance and partial dependence diagnostics, providing a scientifically grounded basis for understanding which variables such as rainfall intensity, hour of day, or proximity to a school dismissal event, most strongly influence departure-time predictions. This directly addresses the panel evaluation requirement for objective metrics with a scientific basis.

## Synthesis

> Recent transportation research from 2022 to the present demonstrates significant advances in spatiotemporal traffic forecasting through graph neural networks, causal attention models, and evolutionary learning architectures capable of capturing nonstationary congestion propagation across urban road networks. These models consistently outperform static baselines by integrating spatial dependencies and temporal variability; however, most remain confined to predictive accuracy evaluation rather than commuter-facing decision implementation. Parallel studies on weather-integrated modeling confirm that precipitation intensity, reduced visibility, and hazard severity introduce nonlinear delay patterns that substantially increase travel-time variability. Empirical assessments of navigation application programming interface outputs, including findings from Peer et al. (2025) and Bastarianto et al. (2025), validate deterministic mapping services as practical real-time routing engines while revealing consistent contextual variability under peak congestion in developing-country road environments, reinforcing the necessity of structured interpretation rather than direct reliance on raw estimated time of arrival outputs. Behavioral research on departure-time decision-making indicates that commuters respond measurably to reliability information and delay risk signals. Concurrent developments in explainable artificial intelligence and large language model integration suggest that generative systems are most defensible when layered over validated analytical outputs.

> The Transync system is positioned within this literature as follows. The shift from a deterministic weighted delay algorithm to an XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model aligns with the gradient-boosted tabular learning paradigm validated by Chen and Guestrin (2016) and Shwartz-Ziv and Armon (2022). The choice of quantile regression over point estimation aligns with the foundational statistical framework of Koenker and Bassett (1978) and addresses the concern raised during panel evaluation regarding the validation of vague accuracy claims. The integration of SHAP-based interpretability following Lundberg and Lee (2017) provides a scientifically grounded basis for objective metrics. The retention of Claude Sonnet 4.6 as a constrained advisory layer over structured outputs remains consistent with the bounded-role recommendation of Wandelt et al. (2024) and the findings summarized in Beyond Words (2025). Together, these positioning choices establish that the Transync system advances rather than departs from the literature surveyed in this chapter.

# Chapter 3 METHODOLOGY

## Introduction

This chapter presents the comprehensive methodology employed in the design, development, and evaluation of Transync, an intelligent predictive travel advisory system tailored for the urban and semi-urban road networks of Lipa City. It outlines the research design, system development framework, requirements analysis, architectural design, implementation technologies, testing procedures, and deployment strategies utilized throughout the study.

The primary objective of this project is to develop a context-aware commuter advisory system that transcends traditional navigation tools by integrating deterministic routing data, a supervised machine learning residual correction model, and an artificial intelligence interpretive layer. Unlike conventional systems that rely solely on static traffic estimation, Transync synthesizes real-time traffic conditions, meteorological data sourced from the Open-Meteo API, learned local corrections produced by an XGBoost quantile regression model, and curated Lipa-specific disruption inputs into a unified predictive pipeline. This enables the system to generate accurate, personalized departure-time recommendations with calibrated arrival confidence rather than vague point estimates.

By leveraging cloud-based infrastructure and multi-source data integration, the system transforms raw structured inputs into actionable insights for commuters. The advisory generation layer is powered by Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.6 language model, which interprets the deterministic routing baseline, the supervised quantile correction, and the retrieved Lipa context into human-readable travel recommendations. The methodology ensures that each component, from data ingestion to advisory generation, is systematically designed to achieve high reliability, scalability, and contextual accuracy, aligning with the study's objective of improving travel efficiency and decision-making in Lipa City.

## Research and Development Design

This study employs a design-and-development research design, which focuses on the systematic analysis, design, development, and evaluation of a software system intended to address a specific user need. This approach is appropriate for the study because the primary objective is not only to examine an existing problem in commuter navigation but also to develop and validate a functional software solution for the target user group. The research design follows the System Development Life Cycle framework, which consists of the key phases of requirements analysis, system design, development, testing, and deployment. Each phase contributes to ensuring that the system meets the functional and non-functional requirements identified during the early stages of the study. The specific execution of these phases within the chosen development framework is detailed in the succeeding sections of this chapter.

## Project Scope and Boundaries

### Scope

The scope of this study encompasses the design, development, and functional validation of Transync as a cloud-based predictive travel advisory system for the road networks of Lipa City. To clearly define the boundaries of the project, the scope is articulated across six dimensions.

Functional scope. The system covers route computation with estimated time of arrival differentiation for private cars and motorcycles via a single XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model. It supports calibrated P10, P50, and P90 arrival predictions; a departure-time-given-arrival recommendation algorithm; multi-stop itinerary planning with user-specified dwell times at each stop; alternate route generation; real-time travel advisory generation with retrieval-augmented Lipa context; and five-tier graceful API failure fallback. 

Technical scope. The system utilizes the Google Maps Platform for deterministic routing, the Open-Meteo API for meteorological data retrieval, and the Anthropic API with Claude Sonnet 4.6 as the artificial intelligence advisory module. The predictive correction layer is implemented as a Python FastAPI microservice running the XGBoost quantile regression model. The frontend is delivered as both a Next.js mobile-first web application and a Flutter native Android client; the backend is built with Node.js and Express, supported by a SQLite database for data persistence and a derived training corpus. 

Data scope. The system ingests real-time traffic density data from the Google Maps Platform, current meteorological data from the Open-Meteo API, and manually encoded contextual disruption inputs maintained in the lipa\_context\_events table. The system additionally persists every Google Maps API response, every Open-Meteo snapshot, every user-initiated trip, and every completed trip's actual duration into a structured training corpus that serves as the input for supervised machine learning correction. 

User scope. The primary users of the system are students and daily commuters in Lipa City, particularly those traveling along high-traffic corridors within and around the city center. The system is designed for individual, non-commercial use by prototype-stage participants, with a confirmed validation group of thirty User Acceptance Testing participants.

Geographic scope. The system is geographically confined to the internal arterial road network of Lipa City, Batangas. It does not extend to intercity travel dynamics or major expressways including the STAR Tollway.

Domain scope. This project operates within the domain of intelligent transportation systems, specifically focusing on commuter advisory and predictive navigation for a mid-sized, rapidly urbanizing secondary city in the Philippines.

### Not Included in the Scope

Despite its comprehensive design, the system operates within defined limitations to ensure feasibility. The study does not include the analysis of pedestrian or non-motorized transport systems such as cycling. Additionally, it does not incorporate public transportation scheduling data, such as fixed public transport routes or timetables, focusing instead on general travel behavior patterns.

The system is geographically limited to Lipa City and does not extend to inter-city travel or expressway systems such as the STAR Tollway. Furthermore, the implementation does not involve the deployment of physical Internet of Things sensors or traffic monitoring hardware, as it relies entirely on third-party data sources accessed through application programming interfaces. Social authentication via third-party providers such as Gmail, as well as two-factor authentication mechanisms, are not included in the current prototype scope and are identified as features for future development iterations. Native iOS deployment is likewise excluded from the current scope due to platform tooling constraints and is identified as future work. Lastly, the project is developed as a prototype and does not include large-scale public deployment or integration with government infrastructure beyond conceptual applicability.

## Project Development Model and Framework

This project adopted the Agile Scrum development model as its primary project development framework. Agile Scrum is an iterative and incremental software development model that organizes work into short, time-boxed cycles called sprints, each typically lasting two to four weeks. Within each sprint, the team completes a defined set of features drawn from a prioritized product backlog, with each cycle producing a functional and testable increment of the system. The framework is built around three core roles: the Product Owner who defines and prioritizes requirements, the Scrum Master who facilitates the process, and the Development Team who executes the work. Key ceremonies include Sprint Planning, Daily Stand-up, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective, which together ensure continuous alignment, transparency, and adaptation throughout the development lifecycle.

Agile Scrum was selected for the development of Transync for several project-specific reasons. First, the system integrates multiple dynamic third-party data sources including the Google Maps Platform, the Open-Meteo API, and the Anthropic API for Claude Sonnet 4.6, each of which carries independent rate limits, response structures, and integration risks that cannot be fully anticipated at the outset. A rigid sequential model such as Waterfall would not accommodate the iterative debugging and adjustment required when integrating live APIs into a working system. Second, several core features of Transync including the XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model, multi-modal estimated time of arrival differentiation, the departure-time recommendation algorithm, and the artificial intelligence advisory layer require repeated testing and calibration against real traffic and weather data before their accuracy can be validated. Scrum's sprint structure allows these components to be built, tested, and refined in successive cycles rather than locked into a single development pass. Third, the system is developed within a fixed twelve-week timeline with defined milestones, which maps naturally onto the sprint-based delivery structure of Scrum, enabling the team to produce functional increments at each milestone rather than delivering only at the end. Fourth, because the system is a prototype intended for User Acceptance Testing with thirty confirmed participants, early usability feedback is essential to refining the interface and advisory output quality before final evaluation. Scrum's Sprint Review mechanism institutionalizes this feedback loop within the development cycle. This aligns with the modular cloud-native architecture principles identified in the related literature, which advocate for builds that separate data ingestion, routing computation, and advisory generation into distinct, testable layers.

The workflow of the project follows a cyclical process consisting of planning, design, development, testing, review, and refinement. Each sprint focuses on a specific set of functionalities, such as API integration, delay computation, or advisory generation. During Sprint Planning, the development team identifies key objectives and prioritizes system features based on their importance and feasibility. The development phase involves implementing system components according to predefined specifications, while the testing phase ensures that each module performs as expected under various conditions. The Sprint Review stage allows for evaluation and refinement, ensuring that any identified issues are addressed in subsequent iterations.

Timelines and Milestones

The project follows a twelve-week timeframe for Capstone 1, which officially began on January 27, 2026\. A total duration of twelve weeks is allocated across four major milestones, with each sprint targeting a specific deliverable that contributes to the progressive completion of the system.

Milestone 1 at Week 2 marks the approval of the Project Proposal. This milestone encompasses the completion of the research design, requirements analysis, and the initial definition of the system architecture. All stakeholder requirements are documented and the functional and non-functional specifications are finalized during this phase.

Milestone 2 at Week 4 marks the completion of the system design. By this point, the full architecture incorporating the Presentation, Application, Data, and Machine Learning Microservice layers has been defined. The XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model has been formalized, API integration plans for Google Maps Platform, Open-Meteo, and the Anthropic API have been documented, the data infrastructure schema for the training corpus has been specified, and the user interface wireframes have been completed. 

Milestone 3 at Week 7 marks the release of the Alpha Version. At this stage, the core functionalities are operational: route computation via the Google Maps Platform is functional, the Open-Meteo API integration for weather data retrieval is active,the baseline estimated time of arrival computation via the Google Maps Platform is working , and the basic advisory generation pipeline connecting deterministic outputs to the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory module is established. User authentication is fully functional.

Milestone 4 at Week 10 marks the release of the Beta Version. This milestone includes the complete integration of estimated time of arrival differentiation for private cars and motorcycles via the XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model; the activation of the departure-time recommendation algorithm; multi-stop itinerary planning functionality with user-specified dwell times; and the full preparation of User Acceptance Testing instruments and participant recruitment. Weeks 11 to 12 are reserved for User Acceptance Testing, evaluation, and final documentation. 

Following the Capstone 1 defense panel evaluation in April 2026, the project timeline was extended for Capstone 2 to accommodate seven additional implementation phases covering data infrastructure, native Android client development, predictive model training, recommendation algorithm implementation, advisory layer enhancement, and final validation. The Capstone 2 implementation cycle spans Weeks 1 through 13 of the post-panel period, with Phase 7 validation and writeup scheduled for completion in Weeks 11 through 13\.
