3.4 Requirements Analysis

The requirements analysis phase is a critical component of the study, as it defines the functional and operational specifications of the Transync system. This phase ensures that all identified user needs, system behaviors, and performance expectations are clearly articulated and aligned with the objectives of the study. To ensure clarity, consistency, and testability, all requirements are expressed using the standard format of the system shall, which enables precise validation during the testing phase.

Requirements Gathering Techniques

Data for the requirements analysis were obtained through a combination of contextual analysis and user-oriented methods. Interviews were conducted with students and daily commuters in Lipa City to understand common travel challenges, including delays caused by congestion, weather conditions, and unexpected disruptions. Additionally, surveys were utilized to gather quantitative data on travel patterns, preferred transportation modes, and user expectations from a navigation system. These techniques allowed the researchers to identify key functional needs, such as multi-modal estimated time of arrival computation and real-time advisory updates, as well as non-functional requirements related to system performance, usability, and reliability.

Document analysis was additionally employed to examine existing navigation platforms including Google Maps and Waze, identifying specific functional gaps in their treatment of public utility vehicle behavior and localized disruption events within Lipa City. Observational analysis of commuter behavior along major arterial roads such as Jose P. Laurel Highway was conducted to validate the transport mode parameters and stopping behavior coefficients used in the XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model's vehicle-type feature engineering . These techniques ensured that the requirements captured in this section reflect both the limitations of existing tools and the operational realities of the Lipa City commuting environment.

## Functional Requirements

The functional requirements define the core capabilities of the Transync system. These are organized into logical modules to reflect the system's operational structure.

### Authentication and User Management

* FR-01: The system shall allow new users to register by providing a username, email address, and password.

* FR-02: The system shall hash all user passwords using bcrypt with a minimum of twelve salt rounds before storing them in the database.

* FR-03: The system shall allow registered users to log in using either their username or email address together with their password.

* FR-04: The system shall issue a JSON Web Token upon successful login, valid for seven days, to authenticate subsequent requests.

* FR-05: The system shall provide a Stay Signed In option that persists the session token in local storage; when unchecked, the token shall be stored in session storage only.

* FR-06: The system shall verify the user's authentication token on every protected route request via the GET /auth/me endpoint before granting access to the main interface.

* FR-07: The system shall allow authenticated users to sign out, clearing all stored session tokens from both local storage and session storage.

### Travel Planning and Prediction

* FR-08: The system shall allow users to input origin, destination, and optional stopovers.

* FR-09: The system shall allow users to select vehicle type: Car or Motorcycle.

* FR-10: The system shall compute multi-modal estimated times of arrival based on selected vehicle type.

* FR-11: The system shall compute calibrated departure-time recommendations using P10, P50, and P90 quantile predictions from the XGBoost residual correction model at a user-selected confidence level. 

* FR-12: The system shall provide alternative routes with corresponding estimated time of arrival comparisons.

### Data Integration and Processing

* FR-13: The system shall retrieve real-time traffic data from the Google Maps Platform.

* FR-14: The system shall retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API.

* FR-15: The system shall incorporate localized disruption inputs including class suspensions, events, and accidents.

* FR-16: The system shall dynamically update predictions based on new incoming data.

### Advisory and Notification System

* FR-17: The system shall generate real-time travel advisories based on computed delays.

* FR-18: The system shall notify users of sudden disruptions such as class cancellations and road closures.

* FR-19: The system shall provide route recommendations based on current conditions.

### User Interaction

* FR-20: The system shall present results in a user-friendly mobile-first interface.

* FR-21: The system shall allow users to re-calculate routes dynamically.

### Predictive Model Integration 

> The system employs an XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model to produce calibrated estimated times of arrival that reflect current environmental and situational conditions. Rather than applying manually assigned penalty weights, the model learns delay patterns from a locally collected training corpus of trip records, weather snapshots, and Lipa-specific contextual events. The corrected ETA at quantile τ is computed as:

> ETA\_τ \= ETA\_Google(O, D, T) \+ r̂\_τ(x)

> where r̂\_τ(x) is the predicted residual at quantile τ from the 27-feature vector x. Three quantiles are predicted simultaneously: P10, P50, and P90, representing optimistic, typical, and conservative arrival scenarios respectively. The vehicle-type feature within the model captures the mobility differential between private cars and motorcycles, which filter through congested traffic in ways enclosed vehicles cannot, consistent with the intracity congestion patterns documented by Caraos, Montalbo, and Fillone (2023) for Lipa City corridors.

> The model processing flow is as follows:

> 1. Accept user input including route, vehicle type, confidence level, and optional stopovers with dwell times.  
> 2. Retrieve real-time traffic and weather data from their respective APIs and log responses to the training corpus.  
> 3. Identify active Lipa-specific disruption events within the route vicinity via structured SQL retrieval.  
> 4. Build the 27-feature vector from temporal, vehicle, route geometry, weather, and Lipa context features.  
> 5. Call the Python FastAPI machine learning microservice and retrieve P10, P50, and P90 residual predictions.  
> 6. Compute the corrected estimated time of arrival at the user-selected confidence level.  
> 7. Generate the departure-time recommendation via the recommendation algorithm.  
> 8. Pass structured output to the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory module with retrieved Lipa context.  
> 9. Return the human-readable advisory to the user interface.

**Feature Vector Specification**

This section enumerates the twenty-seven features that constitute the input vector to the XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model. Features are grouped into five categories reflecting their conceptual role. Raw features are stored directly in the training\_data table; derived features are computed by the shared Node.js feature engineering module at both training-batch time and inference time, ensuring train-serve consistency. Feature importance is validated post-training via SHAP analysis; features shown to contribute negligibly across the training corpus are candidates for ablation in subsequent revisions.

**Group A: Temporal Features (7)**

Temporal features capture systematic time-of-day and day-of-week bias in the Google Maps baseline. Cyclical sin/cos encoding accelerates learning that hour 23 is adjacent to hour 0 without requiring the model to discover this wraparound from data.

| \# | Feature Name | Type | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | hour\_of\_day | Raw | Base temporal signal (0–23) |
| 2 | day\_of\_week | Raw | Weekday vs weekend behavior (0–6) |
| 3 | is\_weekend | Raw | Binary flag accelerating weekend/weekday partition |
| 4 | is\_holiday | Raw | Philippine national holiday flag; disrupts routine patterns |
| 5 | hour\_sin | Derived | Cyclical hour encoding (sine component) so hour 23 is close to hour 0 |
| 6 | hour\_cos | Derived | Cyclical hour encoding (cosine companion) for full circular representation |
| 7 | is\_rush\_hour | Derived | Set when hour\_of\_day is 7–9 or 17–19 on weekdays; captures Lipa AM/PM peaks |

**Group B: Route Geometry Features (5)**

Route geometry features describe the physical shape and length of the trip. Google's baseline ETA is included as an input feature because the residual prediction is defined relative to it. Origin and destination coordinates are stored in the training\_data table for auditability but are deliberately excluded from the model input to prevent the tree ensemble from overfitting to specific geographic points in a small training corpus.

| \# | Feature Name | Type | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 8 | distance\_meters | Raw | Total route distance from Google Maps Directions |
| 9 | google\_eta\_seconds | Raw | Baseline ETA from Google Maps that the model is correcting |
| 10 | google\_eta\_per\_km | Derived | google\_eta\_seconds ÷ (distance\_meters ÷ 1000); effective speed inverse |
| 11 | haversine\_distance\_meters | Derived | Great-circle origin-to-destination distance |
| 12 | route\_directness\_ratio | Derived | distance\_meters ÷ haversine\_distance\_meters; higher values indicate winding routes |

**Group C: Weather Features (6)**

Weather features are populated from the Open-Meteo API response captured at trip-start time. Both raw continuous rainfall and the discretized precipitation bucket are provided because tree ensembles benefit from having both signals available for splitting.

| \# | Feature Name | Type | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 13 | rainfall\_mm\_per\_hour | Raw | Direct precipitation intensity from the Open-Meteo API |
| 14 | temperature\_c | Raw | Ambient temperature; extreme heat correlates with heavier vehicle usage |
| 15 | visibility\_meters | Raw | Reduced visibility slows vehicle speeds |
| 16 | wind\_speed\_mps | Raw | High winds indicate storms and correlate with disrupted commutes |
| 17 | weather\_condition\_code | Raw | WMO weather code (clear, rain, thunderstorm, etc.) |
| 18 | precipitation\_bucket | Derived | 0=none, 1=light (below 2.5mm/h), 2=moderate (2.5–7.5), 3=heavy (above 7.5); PAGASA-standard thresholds |

**Group D: Lipa Context Features (5)**

Lipa context features encode the presence and severity of local disruption events retrieved from the lipa\_context\_events table by spatial-temporal SQL query. Type-specific booleans allow the model to learn distinct delay profiles for school-dismissal windows, fiesta processions, and road closures rather than collapsing all disruption types into a single aggregate signal.

| \# | Feature Name | Type | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 19 | active\_lipa\_events\_count | Raw | Number of lipa\_context\_events overlapping the trip time and corridor |
| 20 | active\_lipa\_events\_max\_severity | Raw | Highest severity (0–5) among active events; 0 if none |
| 21 | has\_school\_dismissal\_event | Derived | Binary flag for active DLSL/BSU/DepEd dismissal window |
| 22 | has\_fiesta\_event | Derived | Binary flag for active fiesta processions or road closures |
| 23 | has\_road\_closure\_event | Derived | Binary flag for active DPWH or LGU road closures |

**Group E: Vehicle and Interaction Features (4)**

Vehicle-type features and manually engineered interactions accelerate the model's learning of mode-specific delay patterns at small sample sizes. The interaction features encode the empirically established observation that public utility vehicles suffer greater additional delays than private cars during peak-hour and adverse-weather conditions.

| \# | Feature Name | Type | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 24 | vehicle\_is\_motorcycle | Raw | 1 if motorcycle, 0 if car |
| 25 | congestion\_x\_motorcycle | Derived | Congestion-hour indicator: google\_eta\_per\_km scaled by the motorcycle flag, capturing motorcycles' ability to filter through traffic in proportion to measured congestion severity |
| 26 | rush\_hour\_x\_motorcycle | Derived | Interaction: is\_rush\_hour × vehicle\_is\_motorcycle; motorcycles gain the most relative advantage during peak congestion |
| 27 | rain\_x\_motorcycle | Derived | Interaction: precipitation\_bucket × vehicle\_is\_motorcycle; motorcycles are more exposed to and slowed by rain than enclosed vehicles |

Then ADD these new requirements after FR-21:

New Requirements

> FR-22: The system shall provide a departure-time-given-arrival recommendation endpoint that, given a target arrival timestamp, returns the latest viable departure time meeting the target at a user-selected confidence level of P50 or P90.

> FR-23: The system shall support multi-stop trips composed of two to ten intermediate stops, each with a user-specified dwell time between zero and 240 minutes.

> FR-24: The system shall expose three distinct quantile predictions — P10, P50, and P90 — for every route prediction request and clearly label each in the user interface.

> FR-25: The system shall call a Python FastAPI machine learning microservice for residual prediction on every route request, with a maximum timeout of 3,000 milliseconds.

> FR-26: The system shall persist every Google Maps API response, every Open-Meteo snapshot, every trip start, and every trip completion to the SQLite training corpus.

> FR-27: The system shall execute a daily batch job that joins logged data and computes the derived training\_data table.

> FR-28: The system shall query the lipa\_context\_events table on every advisory generation request and inject relevant retrieved events into the Claude Sonnet 4.6 prompt.

> FR-29: The system shall implement a five-tier fallback strategy that ensures the advisory output is never empty even when one or more external APIs fail.

### Five-Tier Fallback Strategy Detail

Each tier is defined by what the commuter still receives, not by which service failed, since several distinct failures can land on the same tier. Every request records its active tier so that resilience becomes a measurable distribution in Chapter 4 rather than an unverified claim. The tiers form a ladder rather than a flat list: each successive tier removes exactly one layer of value — advisory prose, then model precision, then input fidelity, then the window itself, then route freshness — so that what a commuter loses at any given tier can be stated precisely.

| Tier | Commuter Receives | Trigger | Timeout Budget |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | Full window (P10/P50/P90) with generated advisory prose | All services healthy, corpus at or above the training threshold | N/A (baseline) |
| 2 | Model-derived window with templated advisory text in place of generated prose | Anthropic API error, first token beyond 2,000 ms, full stream beyond 6,000 ms, or the Claude API key is unset | 2,000 ms first-token / 6,000 ms full stream |
| 3 | Heuristic window computed from historical residual percentiles grouped by rush hour and vehicle type, rather than the model | ML inference beyond 2,500 ms, a 5xx or connection-refused response, corpus below the training threshold, or a feature-order mismatch at boot | 2,500 ms |
| 4 | Window computed with any missing inputs zero-filled and the row flagged for exclusion from training; advisory drops the line tied to the missing input | Open-Meteo failure, or the lipa\_context\_events retrieval query fails | 1,500 ms |
| 5 | A single unadjusted Google Maps ETA, labelled as such, with no window and no advisory | Tiers 2 and 3 are both active at once, or residual history is empty | N/A |
| 6 | The last successful route for the same origin-destination pair, served from a short-lived in-process cache and labelled stale; if no cached entry exists, the request is refused outright rather than inventing a route | Google Directions itself fails or times out | 3,000 ms |

> FR-30: The system shall provide a native Android client built on Flutter that consumes the same backend API as the existing web client.

New Requirements — Social, Gamification, and Convoy Features (Post-Panel Addendum)

> FR-31: The system shall compute, for each completed trip, the total elapsed time, distance traveled, and average speed on the server from trip start and completion records. Maximum speed shall be computed and retained entirely on the client device from the phone's own continuous location stream during Navigation, and shall never be transmitted to or stored on the server.

> FR-32: The system shall maintain a per-user trip history accessible from the user's profile, summarizing all completed trips with their computed metrics.

> FR-33: The system shall generate a shareable trip summary image ("Trip Rank Card"), rendered client-side, containing the trip's elapsed time, distance, and average speed retrieved from the server, combined with the maximum speed value already held in local device state.

> FR-34: The system shall maintain four city-wide leaderboards ranking users by total completed trips, total submitted disruption reports, verified disruption reports confirmed by other users, and computed Efficiency Score.

> FR-35: The system shall allow registered users to submit disruption reports consisting of a location, category, and where applicable a subtype; each accepted submission shall increment the submitting user's Reports count.

> FR-36: User-submitted disruption reports shall be stored separately from the curated lipa\_context\_events knowledge base and shall require administrator review before being promoted into the retrieval-augmented advisory layer.

> FR-37: The system shall compute each user's Efficiency Score as the ratio of the user's mean trip speed to the citywide median trip speed, both derived entirely from the existing trips table's distance and duration fields, without requiring continuous telemetry.

> FR-38: The system shall refresh leaderboard rankings via the existing nightly batch job at 03:00 PHT, joining trip, report, and score data into a derived user\_leaderboard\_stats table.

> FR-39: The system shall allow a registered user to create a Convoy, becoming its owner, and generating a unique shareable join code and link.

> FR-40: The system shall allow other registered users to request to join a Convoy via the join link; the request shall remain in a pending state until approved or denied by the Convoy owner.

> FR-41: The system shall designate the first approved member to record an arrival as the Convoy's route Leader, distinct from the Convoy owner who created it and approves join requests.

> FR-42: For each approved Convoy member, the system shall periodically transmit the member's current position, distance to destination, and estimated time of arrival to all other approved members of the same Convoy, at a polling interval of no less than ten seconds.

> FR-43: The system shall display each Convoy member's status relative to the route Leader's confirmed path, including arrival status and live ETA.

> FR-44: The system shall allow the Convoy owner to remove a member from an active Convoy.

> FR-45: The system shall reject position-broadcast requests from any user not in an approved state for the requested Convoy.

> FR-46: The system shall discard live position broadcast data upon Convoy completion or dissolution, retaining only trip-level completion records already captured for the training corpus.

> FR-47: The system shall allow a user to confirm or deny another user's disruption report; each user may cast at most one vote per report, a user may not vote on their own report, and a report is marked verified once it receives a minimum threshold of confirming votes from distinct users.

## Non-Functional Requirements Specification

The non-functional requirements define the operational quality of the Transync system by establishing measurable criteria for performance, scalability, usability, reliability, and security.

Performance Requirements. The system shall provide near real-time responses, delivering travel computations and advisories within a minimal latency threshold. The system shall generate estimated time of arrival results and advisory outputs within two to three seconds under normal network conditions. The system shall support at least five concurrent users during prototype evaluation, with architecture designed to scale to twenty or more concurrent users in future production deployment. The system shall optimize API calls and cloud resource consumption by implementing caching mechanisms and minimizing redundant requests to external services. The ML microservice adds negligible additional latency at prototype scale, with inference consistently under 50 milliseconds per prediction. Convoy live-tracking introduces a sustained polling load distinct from one-shot route requests; the system shall support at least one active Convoy of up to four concurrently polling members without degrading route-planning response times beyond the established two-to-three-second threshold, with position broadcast data held in server memory rather than persisted per update to avoid write amplification on the file-based SQLite data layer. 

Scalability Requirements. The system shall be capable of scaling both vertically and horizontally through cloud infrastructure, allowing it to accommodate increasing data loads and user demand. The system shall support increased computational capacity by upgrading cloud instance resources. The system shall support load distribution across multiple instances using cloud-based scaling services. The system shall efficiently manage growing datasets, including historical traffic and weather data, without performance degradation.

Usability Requirements. The system shall be designed with a user-centered interface that is easy to learn and navigate, enabling users to understand and utilize its features within a short period. The system shall allow first-time users to understand and effectively use its core features within five minutes without formal training. The system shall be responsive and accessible across multiple devices, including smartphones and web browsers, ensuring usability for a wide range of users.

Reliability and Availability. The system shall maintain an uptime of at least 99 percent, excluding scheduled maintenance periods. The system shall ensure that all processed data from APIs and user inputs remain accurate, consistent, and free from corruption during transmission and storage.

Security Requirements. The system shall utilize HTTPS and TLS encryption to secure all data transmitted between the client and server. The system shall implement session-based authentication and JSON Web Token validation mechanisms to prevent unauthorized access and ensure secure user interaction. User passwords shall be stored using bcrypt hashing with a minimum of twelve salt rounds.

## Use Cases

This section presents the formal use case specifications for the primary interaction scenarios of the Transync system.

Use Case 1: Plan Route and Receive Advisory

Actor: Commuter (registered user). Preconditions: User is authenticated. System has an active internet connection. Google Maps Platform and Open-Meteo API are available.

Main Flow: 1\) User inputs origin, destination, and vehicle type. 2\) System validates input and sends a POST /route request to the backend. 3\) Backend retrieves real-time traffic data from the Google Maps Platform. 4\) Backend retrieves current meteorological data from the Open-Meteo API. 5\) System calls the Python FastAPI ML microservice to retrieve P10, P50, and P90 quantile residual predictions and applies corrections to the Google Maps baseline ETA.  6\) Structured output is passed to the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory module. 7\) System returns adjusted ETA, risk level, and human-readable advisory to the user interface. 8\) The user reviews the advisory and selects Start Trip or Re-calculate.

Alternative Flows: 3a. Google Maps API is unavailable  System displays an error notification and prompts the user to retry. 6a. Anthropic API fails or returns malformed JSON System activates Fallback Tier 2, generating a deterministic template advisory using quantile values and retrieved Lipa context events, and proceeds without language model output. 

Postconditions: User receives a departure recommendation and adjusted ETA. Advisory is displayed in the advisory tab and bottom navigation HUD.

Use Case 2: Plan Multi-Stop Itinerary

Actor: Private vehicle user (registered user). Preconditions: User is authenticated. At least one stopover has been added to the itinerary.

Main Flow: 1\) User inputs origin, one or more stopovers, and final destination. 2\) The system segments the full route into individual legs. 3\) Backend computes per-leg ETA using the Google Maps Distance Matrix API. 4\) The system calls the ML microservice for quantile residual predictions per leg and applies corrections at the user-selected confidence level.  5\) For any leg where the computed delay exceeds the threshold, the system retrieves an alternate route via Google Maps. 6\) The system aggregates cumulative ETA across all legs, accounting for user-specified dwell times at each intermediate stop.  7\) Claude Sonnet 4.6 generates a consolidated multi-stop advisory. 8\) The user receives a per-leg breakdown and total trip advisory.

Alternative Flows: 5a. No viable alternate route is found  System proceeds with the original leg and flags the high-delay segment in the advisory output.

Postconditions: User receives a full itinerary with per-leg ETAs, a cumulative departure recommendation, and a travel advisory for each segment.

Use Case 3: Receive Live Disruption Advisory

Actor: Commuter (registered user, active trip in progress). Preconditions: User has an active trip in progress.

Main Flow: 1\) System detects a significant change in traffic or weather conditions along the active route. 2\) Backend recomputes the quantile-corrected ETA with updated inputs from the Google Maps Platform, Open-Meteo API, and lipa\_context\_events retrieval. 3\) Claude Sonnet 4.6 generates an updated advisory reflecting the disruption. 4\) The system delivers the live advisory notification through the interface. 5\) The user selects Re-calculate Route or continues on the current route.

Alternative Flows: 2a. Updated data is unavailable due to API rate limiting  System uses the last cached values and flags the advisory as based on recently retrieved data.

Postconditions: User is informed of the disruption and receives an updated departure recommendation or reroute advisory.

Use Case 4: Register and Log In

Actor: New user (registration) or returning user (login). Preconditions: For registration — user has a valid email address not previously registered. For login — a user account exists in the system.

Main Flow: 1\) New user submits username, email address, and password via the registration form. 2\) The system hashes the password using bcrypt with twelve salt rounds and stores the account in the SQLite database. 3\) The system issues a JSON Web Token valid for seven days. 4\) On subsequent visits, the returning user submits credentials via the login form. 5\) The system verifies credentials against stored records and reissues a valid JWT. 6\) User is redirected to the protected main route planning interface.

Alternative Flows: 2a. Email address is already registered  System returns an error and prompts the user to log in instead. 5a. Invalid credentials are submitted  System returns an authentication error. Users may retry.

Postconditions: User is authenticated and granted access to the protected route planning interface. Token is stored according to the Stay Signed In preference selected at login.

Use Case 5: Receive Departure Recommendation

> Actor: Commuter (registered user). Preconditions: User is authenticated; user has a target arrival time and a known origin and destination.

> Main Flow:1) User inputs origin, destination, target arrival time, vehicle type, and confidence level, which defaults to P90. 2\) System validates input and sends a POST /route/recommend-departure request to the backend. 3\) Backend iteratively searches candidate departure times backward from the target arrival in five-minute increments. 4\) For each candidate, backend retrieves the Google Maps baseline ETA, queries the ML microservice for quantile residuals, and computes the predicted arrival at the selected confidence level. 5\) Backend returns the latest viable departure time, along with predicted arrival at P50 and P90 confidence and a Claude-generated advisory. 6\) The user reviews the recommendation and selects Confirm or Adjust.

> 

> Alternative Flows: 3a. Trip infeasible — if no valid departure is found within three hours before target arrival at the selected confidence, the system returns a TripInfeasible response with a clear explanation and an offer to lower the confidence level. 4a. ML service timeout — the system uses the Google Maps baseline ETA without residual correction under Fallback Tier 3 and clearly indicates this in the response.

> Postconditions: User receives a calibrated departure recommendation or a clear infeasibility message.

Figure 3.2: Swimlane Diagram — General Commuter User

This swimlane diagram illustrates how the system manages a typical user request from start to finish. It begins with the commuter inputting their trip details, which the web application or native Android client combines with real-time deterministic data including current traffic from the Google Maps Platform and meteorological data from the Open-Meteo API. The feature vector is passed to the Python FastAPI ML microservice, which returns P10, P50, and P90 quantile residual predictions. Relevant Lipa-specific events are retrieved from the lipa\_context\_events table and injected into the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory prompt alongside the corrected ETA. The model generates a human-readable travel advisory that is returned to the user interface. This flow demonstrates the multi-tier architecture of Transync, showing how deterministic routing, supervised machine learning correction, retrieval-augmented context, and constrained AI advisory generation operate as complementary layers while maintaining a data logging pipeline for continuous model improvement. 

![][image4]

Figure 3.3: Swimlane Diagram — Private Vehicle User with Multi-Stop Itinerary

This swimlane diagram outlines the system's enhanced logic for handling complex travel routes with multiple destinations. It begins with the private vehicle user entering several stops along with user-specified dwell times at each intermediate stop, which the web application or native Android client processes by segmenting the full route into individual legs. For each leg, the backend retrieves the Google Maps Platform baseline ETA and calls the Python FastAPI ML microservice to retrieve P10, P50, and P90 quantile residual predictions conditioned on the departure time, vehicle type, weather conditions, and active Lipa context events for that leg. The multi-stop composition algorithm operates backward from the target arrival time, subtracting dwell times at each intermediate stop to compute the recommended departure time for the full trip. Relevant Lipa-specific disruption events along the route corridor are retrieved from the lipa\_context\_events table and injected into the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory prompt. The process concludes with the generation of a comprehensive multi-stop travel advisory that provides per-leg calibrated arrival estimates and a cumulative departure recommendation, demonstrating the system's ability to scale its predictive capabilities for more demanding travel scenarios while maintaining honest uncertainty communication through quantile-aligned confidence levels. 

## System Architecture and Design

Transync is a cloud-based predictive travel advisory system designed for students and daily commuters in Lipa City, Batangas. It addresses the gap left by existing navigation platforms by providing vehicle-type-aware calibrated estimated times of arrival for private cars and motorcycles; integrating real-time weather and curated local context data; and delivering human-readable departure advisories generated by Claude Sonnet 4.6 over deterministic routing baselines from the Google Maps Platform, supervised machine learning corrections from a dedicated microservice, and retrieved Lipa-specific events from a structured knowledge base. The system is accessed through both a mobile-first web browser interface requiring no installation and a native Android client distributed as a direct-download APK, sideloaded onto participant devices with installation guidance provided during onboarding.

The system architecture of Transync is designed using a multi-tier hybrid architecture that separates core computational responsibilities into structured layers to ensure reliability, interpretability, and graceful degradation. The deterministic component, powered by the Google Maps Platform, is responsible for generating base route calculations and real-time traffic data. The machine learning component, implemented as a Python FastAPI microservice running the XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model, produces calibrated P10, P50, and P90 corrections to the Google Maps baseline ETA. The artificial intelligence layer, implemented through the Claude Sonnet 4.6 language model accessed via the Anthropic API, functions as a constrained reasoning module that interprets structured data inputs from the deterministic routing layer, the quantile correction model, and the retrieval-augmented Lipa context layer to generate human-readable advisories and departure recommendations.

### Chosen Architecture Pattern

The system adopts a Three-Tier Architecture enhanced with a Machine Learning Microservice Tier and an Artificial Intelligence Interpretive Layer, consisting of:

1. Presentation Layer  two parallel clients: the Next.js mobile-first web application and the Flutter native Android application.  
2. Application Layer  Node.js and Express backend.  
3. Data Layer  SQLite database via better-sqlite3.  
4. Machine Learning Microservice Tier  Python FastAPI service running the XGBoost quantile residual correction model.  
5. Artificial Intelligence Interpretive Layer  Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory module accessed via the Anthropic API.

This architectural pattern ensures modularity, scalability, and clean separation of concerns. Deterministic routing, learned residual correction, and probabilistic generative reasoning coexist as independent tiers without compromising system stability.

Figure 3.4: Transync Three-Tier System Architecture Diagram with AI Interpretive Layer

#### Presentation Layer

The Presentation Layer serves as the primary interaction point for commuters and now consists of two parallel clients sharing the same backend API.

The web client is a responsive web-based interface built using Next.js, optimized for mobile-first usage. Server-side rendering enables efficient component-based UI development. The interface enables users to input origin, destination, preferred vehicle type, target arrival time, confidence level, and optional multi-stop itineraries with dwell times. It presents outputs such as recommended departure time, P10, P50, and P90 arrival estimates, multiple route options, and real-time advisory notifications and updates. To ensure usability under real-world commuting conditions, the interface follows strict human-centered design principles, including minimal cognitive load that prioritizes only critical travel data, real-time feedback ensuring users are aware of changing conditions, and context-aware alerts such as rainfall warnings or sudden disruptions.

The native Android client is a Flutter application built using the Flutter SDK, compiled via the Android Gradle build system for Android distribution. The native client provides feature parity with the web client and additionally enables background GPS tracking for arrival auto-detection, push notifications for departure-time reminders, and improved offline behavior via Riverpod and flutter\_secure\_storage. The native client is delimited to the Android platform; iOS deployment is identified as future work and is explicitly out of scope.

#### Application Layer

The Application Layer functions as the core orchestration engine of Transync, deployed using a Node.js and Express backend on Render. This layer performs five critical operations. First, API integration and data aggregation: the system retrieves real-time traffic data from the Google Maps Platform and weather data from the Open-Meteo API, logging every response to the training corpus. Second, deterministic baseline computation: the backend captures the Google Maps Platform baseline estimated time of arrival as the reference signal to be corrected. Third, machine learning microservice invocation: the backend calls the Python FastAPI service for P10, P50, and P90 residual quantile predictions on every route request, with graceful timeout and fallback handling. Fourth, retrieval-augmented context assembly: the backend queries the lipa\_context\_events table via structured SQL based on the route corridor and time window, and assembles the retrieved events into the Claude Sonnet 4.6 prompt. This is deterministic structured retrieval — a time-overlap and radius filter against a relational table — rather than dense or vector-based retrieval, and the system is described as such throughout this document. Fifth, artificial intelligence interpretive advisory generation: the processed data is passed to Claude Sonnet 4.6, which operates as a constrained interpretive module generating departure recommendations, risk-level advisories, and suggested behavioral actions over the structured analytical outputs. Sixth, Convoy coordination: a dedicated route group within the Application Layer manages Convoy creation, owner-approval join requests, and short-interval position polling for approved members, reusing the same JWT authentication middleware that protects every other route and holding live position state in server memory rather than in the SQLite data layer. 

Machine Learning Microservice Tier

The Machine Learning Microservice Tier is a dedicated Python FastAPI service that hosts the trained XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model. It exposes a single primary endpoint, POST /predict, which accepts a 27-feature vector and returns the predicted P10, P50, and P90 residuals in seconds to be added to the Google Maps baseline ETA. The microservice is deployed on Render as a separate service from the Node.js backend, with model artifacts stored as JSON files committed to the repository. The Node.js backend invokes the microservice via HTTP with a 3,000 millisecond timeout; if the call fails or times out, the backend gracefully falls back to returning the raw Google Maps ETA without residual correction under Fallback Tier 3\.

#### 

#### 

#### Data Layer

The Data Layer is responsible for storing application data, the training corpus, and the curated Lipa knowledge base. The system uses SQLite as the database engine, implemented through the better-sqlite3 library for synchronous, file-based data access well suited to the prototype scale of the application. In addition to the users table implemented in Capstone 1, six new tables are introduced in Capstone 2: api\_log, weather\_snapshots, trip\_starts, trip\_completions, training\_data, and lipa\_context\_events. Detailed schema specifications are provided in the Entity Relationship Diagram and Database Design sections. 

#### External Services

The system integrates multiple external services to ensure data accuracy and real-time responsiveness. The Google Maps Platform provides route computation, traffic density data, geocoding, and the Distance Matrix API. The Open-Meteo API supplies environmental variables including precipitation intensity, visibility, and weather condition classifications updated every ten minutes. The Anthropic API provides access to the Claude Sonnet 4.6 language model for advisory generation. All API calls to external services are handled exclusively by the backend server to protect API keys from client-side exposure. The native Android client follows the same backend-mediated pattern.

## Data Flow Diagram

The Data Flow Diagrams illustrate the functional decomposition of Transync, tracing the lifecycle of a travel request from raw user input to a calibrated AI-driven advisory. 

### A. Level 0: Context Diagram Discussion

As shown in Figure 3.6, the Context Diagram defines the system boundary and its relationship with external entities. The system acts as a central processing hub that interacts with external entities to retrieve the route, weather, and advisory data required to fulfill user requests.

The flow is initiated by the Commuter (Registered User), who provides a comprehensive set of trip parameters, specifically the origin, destination, stopovers with dwell times, vehicle type, target arrival time, and confidence level. In exchange, the system returns a processed output consisting of the calibrated P10, P50, and P90 estimated times of arrival, the recommended departure time, risk level, and natural language advisory text.

To generate these outputs, the system initiates a request-response cycle with four entities:

* Google Maps Platform: Supplies base route and traffic data based on the user's destination and stopover inputs.  
* Open-Meteo API: Provides meteorological variables such as precipitation intensity, visibility, temperature, and wind speed relevant to the trip coordinates.  
* Machine Learning Microservice: Receives the 27-feature vector assembled from route, weather, temporal, vehicle-type, and Lipa context features, and returns the predicted P10, P50, and P90 residuals to be applied to the Google Maps baseline ETA.  
* Anthropic Claude API: Receives the structured travel context consisting of the corrected quantile ETAs, the recommended departure time, and the retrieved Lipa-specific events, and returns a natural language advisory that is passed back to the user.


![][image6]

Figure 3.6: Data Flow Diagram — Level 0 (Context Diagram)

### B. Level 1: Internal Process Decomposition

As illustrated in Figure 3.7, the Level 1 DFD decomposes the system into seven specialized processes, highlighting the transformation of user inputs into intelligent outputs through internal data stores and the machine learning microservice.

1\. Secure Access and Data Persistence The lifecycle of a request begins with Process 1.0 (Authentication). This process acts as a mandatory checkpoint where raw credentials are cross-referenced with the Users SQLite database. Only upon the issuance of a validated session does the system permit the flow of trip parameters into the subsequent planning modules.

2\. Parallel Data Acquisition and Caching Strategy Once validated, the request triggers two parallel flows to optimize system performance. Process 2.0 (Route Planning) interacts with the Google Maps Platform to generate the geometric path, retrieve the baseline ETA, and log the full API response to the api\_log table. Process 3.0 (Weather Fetch) retrieves meteorological variables and logs the full response to the weather\_snapshots table. To ensure high responsiveness, this process first checks the in-memory weather cache. If fresh data exists, it bypasses the external API; otherwise, it fetches new data and updates the cache. This strategy reduces redundant calls and improves response latency, comfortably within the Open-Meteo API's free-tier limit of 10,000 calls per day.

3\. Machine Learning Residual Correction The baseline ETA and the assembled 27-feature vector are passed to Process 6.0 (ML Microservice Invocation). This process calls the Python FastAPI machine learning microservice, which applies the trained XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model to return P10, P50, and P90 residual predictions. These quantile corrections are added to the Google Maps baseline ETA to produce calibrated probabilistic arrival estimates. If the microservice is unavailable or times out, the system gracefully falls back to the raw Google Maps baseline ETA under Fallback Tier 3\. This process replaces the Capstone 1 weighted delay algorithm, which applied manually assigned penalty weights rather than learned corrections.

4\. Lipa Context Retrieval Concurrently with Process 6.0, Process 7.0 (Lipa Context Retrieval) executes a structured SQL query against the lipa\_context\_events table, filtering by temporal overlap with the trip window and geographic proximity to the route corridor. Up to five most relevant events sorted by severity and recency are returned to Process 5.0 for injection into the advisory prompt.

5\. Interpretive Synthesis The corrected quantile ETAs, the recommended departure time, and the retrieved Lipa context events are passed to Process 5.0 (Advisory Generation). This process interfaces with the Claude Sonnet 4.6 model under a constrained system prompt that restricts the model to interpreting the structured analytical outputs rather than performing routing logic independently. The model translates the numerical findings and local context into a natural language advisory containing the departure recommendation and risk warnings, which is then transmitted back to the commuter through the web or native Android interface.

![][image7]

Figure 3.7: Data Flow Diagram — Level 1

## Entity Relationship Diagram

The database schema of the Transync system has been substantially expanded in Capstone 2 to support the training data pipeline, the predictive model, and the retrieval-augmented advisory layer. The Capstone 1 prototype contained one implemented table supporting user authentication and one planned but unimplemented route\_queries table. The Capstone 2 schema introduces six additional operational tables, superseding the planned route\_queries table with a fully implemented data infrastructure.

The twelve tables in the Capstone 2 schema — seven from the original design plus five added in this addendum — are as follows:

users — stores registered user accounts with bcrypt-hashed passwords. Implemented in Capstone 1 and unchanged in Capstone 2\.

api\_log — stores every Google Maps Directions API response with route polyline, baseline ETA, distance, vehicle type, and full response JSON. Introduced in Capstone 2\.

weather\_snapshots — stores every Open-Meteo API response captured at trip-start coordinates. Introduced in Capstone 2\.

trip\_starts — anchors a user-initiated trip to a specific api\_log and weather\_snapshots record. Introduced in Capstone 2\.

trip\_completions — records the actual duration, end coordinates, completion method, and optional user feedback for each completed trip. Introduced in Capstone 2\.

training\_data — a derived table populated by the daily batch job that joins trip completions with their corresponding API log and weather snapshot records, computes the 27-feature vector, and stores the residual as the machine learning target. Introduced in Capstone 2\.

lipa\_context\_events — a curated table of Lipa-specific events including LGU advisories, school dismissal schedules, fiesta and payday calendars, market day patterns, road closures, and accidents, used by both the retrieval-augmented advisory layer and as features in the predictive model. Introduced in Capstone 2\.

The relationships between tables are as follows. Each user may have many trip\_starts. Each trip\_start references exactly one api\_log record and exactly one weather\_snapshots record. Each trip\_start may have at most one trip\_completion. Each trip\_completion produces exactly one training\_data row after batch processing. The lipa\_context\_events table is a standalone table joined ad hoc by spatial-temporal query at retrieval time and is not linked by foreign key to the transactional tables.

![][image8]

Figure 3.8: Entity Relationship Diagram

## Database Design

The Transync system uses SQLite as its database engine, managed through the better-sqlite3 library for synchronous, file-based data access. The database schema has been expanded from one table in Capstone 1 to twelve tables in Capstone 2 to support the training data pipeline, the predictive model, the retrieval-augmented advisory layer, and the Trip Rank Card, Leaderboard, and Convoy features added in this addendum. ## Retention Policy

## API log and weather snapshot records are retained for six months in full detail, then pruned to records joined with trip completions. Trip starts, trip completions, training data, and lipa context events are retained indefinitely. User identifiers in api\_log and trip\_starts are hashed to anonymized form after thirty days.

## Schema Migration

## A single migration script, migrations/001\_add\_training\_infrastructure.sql, creates the six new tables, adds appropriate indices on timestamps and foreign keys, and is applied automatically on backend startup if not already applied, tracked in a schema\_migrations table. No data backfill is required because the new tables are purely additive.

## New Tables — Social, Gamification, and Convoy Features

The database schema is further extended in this addendum with five new tables supporting the Trip Rank Card, Leaderboard, and Convoy features. Live Convoy position data is deliberately excluded from this schema and held in server memory only, per the Application Layer design and the associated Performance Requirement, to avoid write amplification on the file-based SQLite data layer.

## user\_leaderboard\_stats Table

A derived table, refreshed by the same nightly batch job that populates training\_data, joining completed trips, accepted disruption reports, and per-trip efficiency calculations into a single per-user summary row used to render the four leaderboard categories.

| Field | Data Type | Description | Constraints |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| user\_id | INTEGER | Reference to users | PK, FK, NOT NULL |
| total\_trips | INTEGER | Total completed trips | NOT NULL |
| total\_reports | INTEGER | Total accepted disruption reports | NOT NULL |
| reports\_verified | INTEGER | Count of this user's disruption reports confirmed by other distinct users; feeds the Useful board | NOT NULL |
| efficiency\_score | REAL | Ratio of this user's mean trip speed to the citywide median trip speed, both computed from the trips table; no telemetry required | NOT NULL |
| last\_updated | DATETIME | Timestamp of last nightly batch refresh | NOT NULL |
| total\_distance\_km | REAL | Sum of distance across all completed trips; efficiency numerator support | NOT NULL, DEFAULT 0.0 |
| accuracy\_ratio | REAL | Ratio of verified to total submitted reports; displayed beside the Useful board | NOT NULL, DEFAULT 0.0 |
| contribution\_tier | TEXT | Spotter, Road Watcher, Route Guardian, Traffic Sentinel, or Lipa Roadkeeper, derived from reports\_verified | Nullable |

The contribution\_tier field is derived from reports\_verified against the ladder below, recomputed in the same nightly refresh that populates the rest of this table.

| Tier | Verified Reports Required |
| :---- | :---- |
| Spotter | 5 |
| Road Watcher | 25 |
| Route Guardian | 75 |
| Traffic Sentinel | 150 |
| Lipa Roadkeeper | 300 |

## convoys Table

| Field | Data Type | Description | Constraints |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| id | INTEGER | Primary key | PK, Auto-increment, NOT NULL |
| owner\_user\_id | INTEGER | Convoy creator; the sole approver of join requests | FK, NOT NULL |
| join\_code | TEXT | Unique shareable code, e.g. LIPA-7F3K | Unique, NOT NULL |

| created\_at | DATETIME | Convoy creation timestamp | NOT NULL |
| expires\_at | DATETIME | created\_at plus twelve hours | NOT NULL |

Ownership and route leadership are deliberately separate roles: the owner is whoever created the Convoy and is the sole approver of join requests, while the leader is simply whichever approved member arrives first, whose confirmed route other members then trace. The two are frequently the same person but are not required to be.

## convoy\_members Table

| Field | Data Type | Description | Constraints |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| id | INTEGER | Primary key | PK, Auto-increment, NOT NULL |

UNIQUE(convoy\_id, user\_id). Joining by code always writes a pending row, never approved — possession of the join link grants nothing until the owner acts, which is the enforcement mechanism behind FR-45.

## disruption\_confirmations Table

Backs FR-47. One row per vote, enforcing at most one vote per user per report and excluding the report author from voting on their own submission. Votes cast more than 500 meters from the reported location are rejected. A report becomes verified once its confirming votes reach the category-specific threshold defined in the table below.

| Field | Data Type | Description | Constraints |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| id | INTEGER | Primary key | PK, Auto-increment, NOT NULL |
| report\_id | INTEGER | Reference to disruption\_reports | FK, NOT NULL |
| user\_id | INTEGER | Voter; must not be the report author | FK, NOT NULL |
| vote | TEXT | confirm or deny | NOT NULL |
| voted\_at | DATETIME | Vote timestamp | NOT NULL |
| distance\_from\_report\_m | REAL | Voter's distance from the reported location at time of vote; votes beyond 500m are rejected | NOT NULL |

## Disruption Report Categories, Expiry, and Verification Thresholds

Each report category carries its own time-to-live and confirmation threshold, reflecting how quickly that class of disruption typically resolves. The weather subgroup substitutes a landslide subtype for the more commonly cited ice hazard, since Lipa is tropical and the Malarayat and Mt. Malepunyo approach roads are genuinely landslide-prone — a localization decision grounded in the same corridor conditions documented in Chapter 2\.

| Category | Subtypes | Expires After | Confirmations to Verify |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| traffic\_jam | Moderate, Heavy, Standstill | 30 minutes | 2 |
| police | Visible, Hidden, Other Side | 45 minutes | 2 |
| crash | Minor, Major, Other Side | 90 minutes | 2 |
| hazard | grouped: on\_road, shoulder, weather | 120 minutes | 2 |
| closure | none, submits immediately | 180 minutes | 3 |

Deduplication runs at submission: a new report of the same category within 150 meters and 10 minutes of an existing active report is written with dedup\_parent\_id set and counted as a confirmation of the parent rather than a new pin, preventing multiple commuters passing the same incident from producing duplicate markers.

## User Interface Design

The user interface of Transync follows a mobile-first design philosophy, with all layouts and interactions optimized for smartphone viewport dimensions. The interface is built using Next.js and styled with inline CSS following the Midnight Indigo design system, which establishes a consistent visual language across all screens. Core design principles applied throughout include minimal cognitive load by surfacing only critical travel information, real-time visual feedback that keeps users informed of system state, and context-aware alerts that communicate risk level through color-coded badges.

The login page presents a frosted glass card on a dark background using a base color of \#020617, with a three-phase entrance animation that introduces the Transync logo before revealing the authentication form. The route planner interface is structured as a full-screen map with an overlay planner card that accepts origin and destination inputs. The destination field uses the Google Places Autocomplete widget biased to the Lipa City bounding box to constrain suggestions to locally relevant addresses.

Upon receiving a route result, the system populates a Live Destination Preview card within the planner overlay, displaying the adjusted ETA, risk level badge, and the Claude Sonnet 4.6 generated advisory text. When the user initiates a trip, the planner overlay is dismissed and a bottom navigation HUD slides into view, showing the active ETA, a traffic status badge, and the advisory summary. The HUD includes a drag handle for minimizing and expanding, and an End Trip control that returns the user to the planner. Two floating action buttons  a recenter button and a gyroscope toggle  remain accessible during active navigation.

Security Architecture

The security architecture of Transync is designed to protect both system integrity and user data while maintaining high availability. All communications between the client interface and backend services are secured using HTTPS with TLS encryption. User authentication is managed through JSON Web Tokens with a seven-day expiration, validated on every protected endpoint through the Authorization Bearer header mechanism. The system implements input validation mechanisms to prevent malformed or malicious queries from affecting system performance. User passwords are stored exclusively as bcrypt hashes with twelve salt rounds. Two-factor authentication and social login via third-party providers are identified as features for future development iterations and are not included in the current prototype scope.

Deployment Architecture

Transync follows a cloud-based deployment model where all backend services, APIs, and databases are hosted within a unified cloud infrastructure. The architecture supports real-time API communication, backend-driven computation of routes and advisories, and dynamic scaling based on user demand.

The system is deployed across two parallel services on Render. The Node.js and Express backend serves both the Next.js web client and the Flutter Android client through a shared REST API, with the SQLite database maintained as a file-based store via better-sqlite3 on an attached persistent disk. The Python FastAPI machine learning microservice is deployed as a separate, stateless Render service in the same project, loading the trained XGBoost model artifact on startup and serving quantile residual predictions via the POST /predict endpoint. The Node.js backend communicates with the microservice over HTTP via the ML\_SERVICE\_URL environment variable.

The native Android client is built via the Android Gradle build system and distributed to the thirty User Acceptance Testing participants as a direct-download APK, sideloaded onto participant devices with installation guidance provided during onboarding. Web users continue to access the system through mobile browsers without installation. iOS distribution is explicitly out of scope for the current prototype.

For the purposes of this prototype, the deployment environment is configured to prioritize development velocity and stability for the target user base of up to thirty User Acceptance Testing participants, while maintaining the architectural principles described in this chapter. Monthly XGBoost model retraining is scheduled as new trip data accumulates in the training corpus.

![][image17]

Figure 3.9: Transync Deployment Architecture Diagram

Scalability and Performance Considerations

To ensure long-term viability, the system incorporates several performance optimization strategies. Weather data responses are cached per geographic coordinate for a period of five to ten minutes to reduce redundant Open-Meteo API calls and improve response latency, comfortably within the free tier's usage limits. Route computations are only triggered on user-initiated requests and not on continuous background polling. A ten-minute coordinate-bucket cache is implemented for Google Maps API responses to reduce the per-recommendation cost of the iterative departure-time search, which typically evaluates twenty-four to thirty-six candidate departures per request. The Python FastAPI machine learning microservice operates with inference latency consistently under fifty milliseconds per prediction at prototype scale, adding negligible overhead to the overall response time. The Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory module is called once per route request and returns a structured JSON response. In the event of partial or complete API failure, the five-tier fallback strategy ensures the user interface never presents an empty advisory state, with each fallback tier emitting a source field to enable monitoring of degradation frequency in production. 

Design Constraints and Assumptions

The system assumes stable API availability and internet connectivity on the part of the user. It is constrained by the accuracy and limitations of third-party data sources, which may introduce variability in predictions. Specific constraints include dependence on stable internet connectivity for real-time data retrieval, reliance on third-party application programming interfaces which may introduce variability in data accuracy, a limited geographic scope confined to Lipa City, the modest training data accumulation window of the Capstone 2 implementation period which affects the initial predictive model quality, and the manual curation requirement for the lipa\_context\_events knowledge base which introduces a maintenance dependency on team members for ongoing accuracy. The machine learning model's predictive quality is expected to improve progressively as the training corpus grows through continued system usage. 

3.6 Development Tools and Technologies

The development of Transync utilizes a carefully selected technology stack designed to support real-time computation, scalability, and artificial intelligence integration. Each tool and technology was selected based on three criteria: compatibility with the system's architectural requirements, availability of a free or prototype-appropriate tier, and the development team's ability to implement and maintain it within the twelve-week project timeline.

Development Environment

The system was developed using Visual Studio Code as the primary code editor, chosen for its lightweight architecture, extensive extension support, and native integration with Git version control. API endpoint testing and validation were conducted using Postman, which allows the team to simulate HTTP requests against the backend and verify response structures before connecting them to the frontend. The Python FastAPI machine learning microservice was developed and tested in a separate virtual environment using the same Visual Studio Code setup, with the XGBoost training scripts executed locally on a Ryzen 7 7700 CPU development machine. 

Programming Languages

The system was developed using JavaScript, TypeScript, and Python as its primary programming languages. JavaScript is used across the full stack, providing consistency between the frontend Next.js components, the Flutter Android client, and the backend Node.js and Express server. TypeScript is applied throughout the frontend codebase to enforce type safety, reduce runtime errors in component props and API response handling, and improve code readability during iterative development. Python is used exclusively for the machine learning microservice, chosen for its mature ecosystem of data science and machine learning libraries including XGBoost, pandas, scikit-learn, and SHAP. 

Frameworks and Libraries

The web frontend interface is built using Next.js, a React-based framework chosen for its server-side rendering capabilities, file-based routing, and native support for environment variable management through the NEXT\_PUBLIC prefix convention. Next.js enables the single-loader pattern used in Transync, where the Google Maps JavaScript API is loaded once in the root page component and passed as a prop to child components, preventing duplicate initialization errors.

The native Android client is built using the Flutter SDK. Key dependencies include google\_maps\_flutter for map rendering, geolocator for background GPS tracking, flutter\_local\_notifications for departure-time push notifications, flutter\_secure\_storage for encrypted token storage, Riverpod for server state management and offline caching, Riverpod for reactive state management, and Flutter ThemeData for styling using the Midnight Indigo theme conventions established in the web client. Release APKs are produced via the standard Android Gradle build toolchain and distributed directly to participants as a downloadable file for manual installation.

The backend is implemented using Node.js with the Express framework. Express was selected for its minimal footprint, straightforward REST API routing, and broad compatibility with the Node.js middleware ecosystem. The backend uses the cors package to enforce cross-origin resource sharing restrictions, allowing requests only from the configured frontend URL. Password hashing is handled by bcryptjs with twelve salt rounds, and user session tokens are managed using the jsonwebtoken library with a seven-day expiration policy. The better-sqlite3 library provides synchronous, file-based SQLite access for both the application database and the training corpus tables.

The machine learning microservice is built using Python and FastAPI, chosen for its high-performance asynchronous request handling and automatic OpenAPI documentation generation. The XGBoost library provides the quantile regression residual correction model, configured with the reg:quantileerror objective and three quantile targets. The SHAP library is used for model interpretability analysis. The shared feature engineering logic is implemented as a Node.js module called by both the training data batch job and the inference endpoint to ensure train-serve consistency.

**Hyperparameter Selection and Tuning**

Hyperparameters for the XGBoost quantile regression model are selected via five-fold time-series cross-validation on the training partition of the temporally held-out split. The search space covers learning\_rate in the range 0.01 to 0.15, max\_depth from 4 to 8, min\_child\_weight from 1 to 5, subsample from 0.7 to 1.0, and colsample\_bytree from 0.7 to 1.0. Selection prefers hyperparameter combinations that minimize the mean pinball loss averaged across the three quantile targets, with a secondary preference for shallower trees to reduce overfitting risk given the modest training corpus size. Final selected values are reported alongside cross-validation scores in the evaluation chapter.

**Cold-Start Behavior and Minimum Training Corpus**

The XGBoost model requires a minimum training corpus of five hundred completed trip records before it is promoted to serve production predictions. During the initial data-collection window, when the training corpus is below this threshold, the machine learning microservice returns a null residual response and the backend gracefully falls back to Fallback Tier 3, which returns the raw Google Maps baseline estimated time of arrival without residual correction. This threshold is calibrated on the principle that gradient-boosted trees require at least an order of magnitude more training samples than input features to avoid severe overfitting, giving approximately eighteen training samples per feature at the minimum threshold.

**Retraining Trigger and Model Promotion Policy**

The XGBoost model is retrained on a scheduled monthly cadence via a manual training script run on the development environment, with retraining also triggered on demand when the training corpus grows by twenty percent since the last training run. Every candidate model is evaluated against the previously deployed model on a held-out temporal test partition using mean absolute error on the P50 quantile as the primary promotion criterion. A candidate model is promoted to production only when it achieves a lower mean absolute error than the deployed model with statistical significance established by paired bootstrap resampling at the ninety-five percent confidence level. Otherwise, the deployed model is retained and the candidate is archived for later review.

**Model Versioning and Rollback**

Every trained model is persisted with an incrementing semantic version identifier of the form major-dot-minor and includes an accompanying manifest recording the training corpus size, feature schema hash, training timestamp, and cross-validation scores. The trip\_starts table records the model version responsible for each recorded prediction, enabling per-version accuracy auditing and clean rollback in the event that a promoted model exhibits regressions detected in post-deployment monitoring. Rollback is accomplished by pointing the FastAPI service at the previous model artifact file and restarting the microservice; no schema changes or backend redeployment are required.

The @anthropic-ai/sdk npm package is used to integrate the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory module into the Express backend. The SDK provides a typed interface to the Anthropic Messages API, enabling the team to construct constrained system prompts that enforce structured JSON advisory responses, inject retrieved Lipa context events, and activate the appropriate fallback tier with proper error handling logic.

Database Technologies

The system uses SQLite as its database management system, implemented through the better-sqlite3 library. SQLite was selected over cloud-hosted database services for three reasons specific to this prototype. First, it requires zero configuration  the database file is created automatically on the first server start, eliminating setup overhead during development. Second, better-sqlite3 operates synchronously, which avoids asynchronous complexity in a prototype context where concurrent write operations are not a concern at five-user scale. Third, it imposes no cost, network dependency, or external service dependency, making the data layer fully self-contained within the deployment environment. In Capstone 2, the SQLite schema is extended with six additional tables supporting the training data pipeline and the retrieval-augmented advisory layer. A schema migration script applied automatically on backend startup ensures that the new tables are created idempotently without requiring manual intervention. The training\_data table is populated by a daily batch job running at 03:00 PHT via an in-process scheduled task (node-cron) running within the backend service itself, which joins trip completions with their corresponding API log and weather snapshot records and computes the 27-feature vector for each completed trip. Running the batch job in-process, rather than as a separate scheduled service, guarantees direct access to the same persistent disk as the rest of the backend without introducing a cross-service dependency. 

Version Control and Collaboration Tools

Source code versioning is managed using Git, with the project repository hosted on GitHub. Git enables the team to track incremental changes, maintain a commit history aligned with sprint milestones, and recover from breaking changes through branch management. All environment variable files are excluded from version control via .gitignore to prevent API key exposure.

A critical security design decision in the technology stack is the two-key architecture used for the Google Maps Platform. A browser-restricted API key is used exclusively for loading the map user interface and the Places Autocomplete widget in the frontend. A server-side API key with IP address restriction is used for all backend API calls including route generation, geocoding, and estimated time of arrival computation. This separation ensures that sensitive server-side credentials are never exposed to the client browser, preventing unauthorized API usage.

## Testing and Validation

The testing strategy for Transync is designed to ensure the system meets both functional and non-functional requirements under realistic operating conditions. The process follows a tiered approach aligned with the specific objectives established in Chapter 1\. For Capstone 2, the testing strategy has been substantially expanded to include model performance testing, end-to-end recommendation testing, and a rigorous quantitative evaluation methodology that addresses the panel evaluation requirements for scientifically grounded metrics, confusion matrix evaluation, and validation of accuracy claims. 

### Types of Testing Conducted

Unit Testing is performed on individual modules such as the baseline ETA computation, the XGBoost quantile residual correction model, the feature engineering module, the departure-time recommendation algorithm, and API data retrieval functions, ensuring each component produces correct outputs independently. Test cases validate accurate differentiation of estimated times of arrival based on vehicle type, proper quantile residual predictions under varying input conditions, zero train-serve skew between the training batch job and the inference endpoint, and correct computation of the departure-time recommendation across single-leg and multi-stop trip configurations.

Integration Testing evaluates the interaction between all system tiers. It verifies that traffic data and weather inputs are correctly logged to the api\_log and weather\_snapshots tables on every route request, that the Node.js backend correctly calls the Python FastAPI machine learning microservice and handles timeout and fallback conditions, that retrieved lipa\_context\_events are correctly injected into the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory prompt, that the structured JSON response from the Anthropic API is correctly parsed and rendered in both the web and native Android client interfaces, and that each fallback tier activates correctly under the corresponding failure condition.

System Testing assesses the complete end-to-end workflow from user input to final advisory across both client platforms, focusing on system responsiveness and reliability. Test cases validate real-time updating of advisories during sudden disruptions, correct generation of alternative routes and multi-stop itineraries with user-specified dwell times, system response time against the two-to-three-second latency threshold established in the non-functional requirements, and correct behavior of the native Android client including background GPS arrival detection and push notification delivery.

Model Performance Testing validates the XGBoost quantile residual correction model against three baselines  the naive mean residual baseline, the hour-of-day grouped mean baseline, and the raw Google Maps ETA baseline  using a temporally held-out test set. Evaluation metrics include mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and mean absolute percentage error per quantile, empirical quantile coverage at P10, P50, and P90, a three-class confusion matrix with per-class precision, recall, and F1 scores, and paired bootstrap resampling with 10,000 iterations to produce ninety-five percent confidence intervals on every reported metric.

End-to-End Recommendation Testing validates the departure-time recommendation algorithm against both synthetic and live trip scenarios, confirming that the algorithm correctly identifies the latest viable departure time for feasible trips, returns a clear TripInfeasible response for infeasible targets, and correctly aggregates per-leg quantile predictions across multi-stop trips with user-specified dwell times.
