### 

### User Acceptance Testing

User Acceptance Testing is conducted with a confirmed group of thirty participants consisting of students and daily commuters who are familiar with Lipa City road conditions and regularly travel through the corridors covered by the system. Participants are recruited from De La Salle Lipa and surrounding academic and commercial areas within the city center. Each participant interacts with the deployed prototype under real commuting conditions and completes a structured evaluation instrument upon completion.

The evaluation focuses on seven dimensions: accuracy of route and departure-time recommendations, clarity of the quantile-based confidence communication, ease of use of the mobile-first web interface and native Android client, usefulness and clarity of advisory outputs, reliability and performance under real commuting conditions, overall satisfaction with the system, and engagement with the Trip Rank Card, leaderboard, and Convoy features. To ensure a comprehensive assessment, the study employs a dual-instrument approach consisting of a system-specific User Acceptance Testing questionnaire and the standardized System Usability Scale.

The custom UAT instrument is designed to evaluate system-specific features including route planning, multi-modal estimated time of arrival accuracy, the departure-time-given-arrival recommendation function, multi-stop itinerary planning with dwell times, integration of traffic and weather data, the effectiveness of AI-generated travel advisories augmented with Lipa-specific context, and the clarity of the P50 and P90 confidence level selector. The instrument consists of thirty-nine items across seven dimensions: Functional Suitability, Advisory Quality, Usability and Interface Design, Performance and Reliability, Security and Trust, Social and Gamification Features, and Overall Satisfaction. A new item, A.1.7, is included to specifically evaluate whether the system clearly communicates the range of possible arrival times between typical and conservative estimates.

The System Usability Scale is used to measure perceived usability and learnability, providing a standardized benchmark for comparison. A System Usability Scale score of at least 70, corresponding to an acceptable or good usability rating, is established as the acceptance benchmark for this study, consistent with the success threshold defined in the specific objectives of Chapter 1\.

### Evaluation Instrument and Interpretation

The system-specific UAT questionnaire consists of thirty-nine items grouped into seven evaluation dimensions, with each item rated using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree). Mean scores are computed for each dimension to assess overall system performance and user acceptance. The seven dimensions are Functional Suitability, Advisory Quality, Usability and Interface Design, Performance and Reliability, Security and Trust, Overall Satisfaction, and Social and Gamification Features. Per-item means are reported in tabular form with standard deviations. The new Capstone 2 item A.1.7, which evaluates whether the system clearly communicates the range of possible arrival times between typical and conservative estimates, is highlighted separately as a direct indicator of the quantile confidence selector's user experience effectiveness.

The System Usability Scale questionnaire consists of ten alternating positive and negative statements evaluated using the same five-point Likert scale. Raw scores are converted to a standardized scale ranging from 0 to 100 using the established SUS scoring formula. Scores of 70 and above are considered acceptable usability, while scores of 85 and above are interpreted as excellent.

The model evaluation methodology produces quantitative results reported across four tracks. The regression performance track reports mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and mean absolute percentage error per quantile on the held-out test set, with ninety-five percent confidence intervals computed via paired bootstrap resampling across 10,000 iterations. The quantile calibration track reports empirical coverage at P10, P50, and P90 to validate that the model's probabilistic claims are accurate. The classification performance track reports a three-class confusion matrix with per-class precision, recall, and F1 scores derived from the early, on-time, and late framing. The interpretability track reports SHAP-based ranked feature importance and partial dependence diagnostics for the top three features.

In addition to quantitative measures, participants provide qualitative feedback on the perceived accuracy of advisory outputs, usability of the interface across both the web and native Android clients, clarity of the departure-time recommendation and confidence level selector, and recommendations for system improvement. This qualitative data supports deeper analysis and interpretation of the quantitative results.

### Evaluation Design

The evaluation instrument was divided into two components:

1. A custom-designed User Acceptance Testing questionnaire, tailored to assess the specific features and innovations of the system  
2. The System Usability Scale (SUS), used to measure overall usability and provide a standardized benchmark

All participants were instructed to use the system and complete both instruments after interaction.

Responses for the custom questionnaire were measured using a five-point Likert scale, defined as follows:

1 – Strongly Disagree  
 2 – Disagree  
 3 – Neutral  
 4 – Agree

## B. System Usability Scale (SUS)

To complement the custom evaluation, the study employed the System Usability Scale, a standardized instrument for assessing perceived usability. The SUS consists of ten statements with alternating positive and negative wording, rated on a five-point Likert scale.

The SUS questionnaire used in this study is presented below:

1. I think that I would like to use this system frequently.  
2. I found the system unnecessarily complex.  
3. I thought the system was easy to use.  
4. I think that I would need the support of a technical person to use this system.  
5. I found the various functions in this system were well integrated.  
6. I thought there was too much inconsistency in this system.  
7. I would imagine that most people would learn to use this system very quickly.  
8. I found the system very cumbersome to use.  
9. I felt very confident using the system.  
10. I needed to learn a lot of things before I could get going with this system.

## Scoring and Interpretation

The responses from the custom UAT instrument were analyzed by computing the mean scores for each evaluation category and the overall system rating. Higher mean scores indicate better perceived system performance and user acceptance.

For the System Usability Scale, responses were scored using the standard SUS scoring procedure, resulting in a total score ranging from 0 to 100\. A score of 70 or above was considered acceptable usability, while scores above 85 indicate excellent usability.

The integration of both instruments allows the study to provide a comprehensive evaluation, where the custom questionnaire captures system-specific performance and innovation, and the SUS provides a validated benchmark for overall usability.

## Deployment Environment and Strategy

The Transync platform is deployed using a cloud-based architecture to ensure availability and real-time synchronization for the target user base within Lipa City. The system is deployed across two parallel services on Render. The Node.js and Express backend and the Next.js web frontend are hosted together as the primary Render service, on a paid instance with a persistent disk attached to preserve the SQLite database across deploys and restarts, handling route computation, data logging, recommendation algorithm execution, retrieval-augmented context assembly, and integration with the Claude Sonnet 4.6 advisory module without the need for manual server management. The Python FastAPI machine learning microservice is deployed as a separate, stateless Render service in the same project on the free instance type, loading the trained XGBoost quantile regression model artifact on startup and serving P10, P50, and P90 residual predictions via the POST /predict endpoint. A scheduled health-check ping keeps the microservice warm and avoids cold-start delays against its inference timeout. The Node.js backend communicates with the microservice over HTTP via the ML\_SERVICE\_URL environment variable, with a 3,000 millisecond timeout and graceful Fallback Tier 3 degradation if the service is unavailable.

Data persistence is managed through a file-based SQLite database, enabling structured storage of user account information, the training corpus, and the curated Lipa knowledge base with high-speed synchronous retrieval suitable for the prototype scale of the application. A daily batch job running at 03:00 PHT, scheduled in-process within the backend service via node-cron, processes completed trip records into the derived training\_data table, ensuring the training corpus grows continuously as the system accumulates real-world usage data.

The native Android client is built via the Android Gradle build system and distributed to the thirty User Acceptance Testing participants as a direct-download APK, sideloaded onto participant devices with installation guidance provided during onboarding. Web users continue to access the system through a secure URL on any mobile device with internet connectivity without installation. iOS distribution is explicitly out of scope for the current prototype.

To maintain system integrity, the deployment includes monitoring of external API health for the Google Maps Platform, Open-Meteo, and Anthropic integrations. The five-tier fallback strategy ensures the user interface never presents an empty or broken advisory state, with each fallback tier emitting a source field in the advisory response to enable monitoring of degradation frequency in production. Monthly XGBoost model retraining is scheduled as new trip data accumulates in the training corpus.

## 

## Implementation and User Training

The implementation strategy includes an initial controlled rollout phase where selected User Acceptance Testing participants interact with the system under real commuting conditions across both the web client and the native Android client. Guidance is provided to participants on how to input travel data, interpret advisory outputs, use the confidence level selector to distinguish between typical and conservative arrival estimates, review departure-time recommendations, and navigate the multi-stop itinerary planning interface with dwell time inputs. The system's design goal of allowing first-time users to operate core features within five minutes without formal training, as established in the usability non-functional requirements, governs the simplicity requirements of both client interfaces.

Native Android participants additionally receive brief guidance on enabling background GPS tracking for arrival auto-detection and on permitting push notification delivery for departure-time reminders. Token storage and session persistence are handled automatically via flutter\_secure\_storage and require no user action.

## Maintenance and Support Plan

To ensure long-term functionality within the prototype phase, the system incorporates a structured maintenance strategy that includes continuous monitoring of all external API integrations for availability and response time, monthly retraining of the XGBoost quantile regression residual correction model as new trip completion records accumulate in the training corpus, periodic updates to the lipa\_context\_events knowledge base by team members on a rotating weekly curation schedule, and system performance optimization based on usage patterns observed during User Acceptance Testing. Weather API calls are cached per coordinate location for five to ten minutes to reduce redundant calls and latency, comfortably within the Open-Meteo API free tier threshold of 10,000 calls per day. Google Maps API responses are cached in a ten-minute coordinate-bucket cache to reduce the per-recommendation cost of the iterative departure-time search.

Fallback tier activation frequency is monitored via the source field emitted on every advisory response, enabling the team to identify degraded API conditions and prioritize remediation efforts. Technical support mechanisms are established to address potential issues during the controlled rollout and to ensure uninterrupted system operation throughout the evaluation period. The schema migration system ensures that database updates are applied automatically and idempotently on backend startup, eliminating the need for manual database administration during the maintenance period.
